docs.title: Scanning a package for deprecated wrappers
docs.text:
find_deprecation_wrappers() walks an entire package or module and returns a list of DeprecationWrapperInfo entries, one per deprecated callable discovered. Pass either a module object or a dotted module path string. This is the foundation for all package-wide CI checks.

The following scanning functions accept the same scope options:

  • find_deprecation_wrappers() discovers wrappers.
  • validate_deprecation_expiry() checks removal deadlines.
  • validate_deprecation_policy() checks governance rules.
  • validate_deprecation_chains() detects deprecated targets.
  • validate_mapping_compatibility() reports positional-only mappings.
  • generate_deprecation_table() generates reports.

Their keyword-only exclude argument accepts glob patterns over full dotted module names, such as exclude=["my_package.tests", "*._legacy*"].

The scan never imports a matching package or descends into it. Another module may still import it, but its wrappers are filtered either way. No wrapper reported under a matching module is returned.

Use exclusions to omit test fixtures or a frozen legacy tree from every audit. The CLI reads the same list from --exclude or [tool.pydeprecate] in pyproject.toml. See project configuration.

These six functions also accept include_members, which defaults to True.

Setting Scope include_members=True Deprecated methods, constructors, properties, other descriptors, and deprecated_class proxies bound as class attributes are included. include_members=False Only module-level wrappers are checked.

Every CLI subcommand accepts the matching --no-include-members flag.

Recursive scans execute imports

Recursive scans import every submodule, so module-level side effects run. Any import exception, not just ImportError, skips the submodule. Module-level sys.exit() also skips it.

The scan emits UserWarning: audit: skipped <module>: <exception> and continues. One broken submodule cannot abort the whole CI gate.

The CLI also writes pydeprecate gap: module not audited: <module>: <exception> to stderr for each skipped submodule. This remains visible even when your package silences warnings.

from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package

# Scan an entire package for deprecated wrappers
results = find_deprecation_wrappers(my_package)

# Or scan using a string module path
results = find_deprecation_wrappers("tests.collections.api_deprecated.core")

# Filter to only ineffective wrappers
ineffective = [r for r in results if r.no_effect]
print(f"Found {len(ineffective)} deprecated wrappers with zero impact!")

# Check some results - each item is a DeprecationWrapperInfo dataclass
for r in results[:5]:
    print(f"{r.module}.{r.function}: no_effect={r.no_effect}")
    if r.no_effect:
        print(f"  Warning: This wrapper has zero impact!")
        print(f"  invalid_args: {r.invalid_args}, identity_args_mapping: {r.identity_args_mapping}")
Output: f"Found {len(ineffective)} deprecated wrappers with zero impact!" 
Found 0 deprecated wrappers with zero impact!
tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.ChainedProxyColorEnum: no_effect=False
tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.CrossGuardModuleLevel.old_method: no_effect=False
tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.CrossGuardOldClass.__init__: no_effect=False
tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.CrossGuardSameClass.old_method: no_effect=False
tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DecoratedDataClass: no_effect=False

docs.title: Scanning a misconfigured collection
docs.text:
tests.collections.misconfigured intentionally mixes invalid args, empty mappings, identity mappings, self-references, and target-mode misconfigurations. Use it as a regression fixture to see the audit buckets in one place.

from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers

# For testing purposes, we use the misconfigured test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections import misconfigured as my_package

results = find_deprecation_wrappers(my_package, recursive=False)

invalid_args = [r for r in results if r.invalid_args]
empty_mappings = [r for r in results if r.empty_args_mapping]
identity_mappings = [r for r in results if r.identity_args_mapping]
self_refs = [r for r in results if r.self_reference]
misconfigured_targets = [r for r in results if r.misconfigured_target]
no_effect = [r for r in results if r.no_effect]

print("=== Misconfiguration Report ===")
print(f"Wrappers scanned: {len(results)}")
print(f"Invalid arguments: {len(invalid_args)}")
print(f"Empty mappings: {len(empty_mappings)}")
print(f"Identity mappings: {len(identity_mappings)}")
print(f"Self-references: {len(self_refs)}")
print(f"Misconfigured targets: {len(misconfigured_targets)}")
print(f"No effect: {len(no_effect)}")
Output: f"No effect: {len(no_effect)}" 
=== Misconfiguration Report ===
Wrappers scanned: 14
Invalid arguments: 3
Empty mappings: 7
Identity mappings: 3
Self-references: 1
Misconfigured targets: 6
No effect: 6

Group results by issue type for structured reports — separate hard errors (invalid argument names) from advisory notes (identity mappings):

from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package

results = find_deprecation_wrappers(my_package)

# Group by issue type (using dataclass attribute access)
wrong_args = [r for r in results if r.invalid_args]
identity_mappings = [r for r in results if r.identity_args_mapping]
self_refs = [r for r in results if r.self_reference]

print(f"=== Deprecation Validation Report ===")
print(f"Wrong arguments: {len(wrong_args)}")
print(f"Identity mappings: {len(identity_mappings)}")
print(f"Self-references: {len(self_refs)}")
Output: f"Self-references: {len(self_refs)}" 
=== Deprecation Validation Report ===
Wrong arguments: 0
Identity mappings: 0
Self-references: 0

docs.title: PEP 702-only deprecations
docs.text:
The default scan skips symbols deprecated only with warnings.deprecated or typing_extensions.deprecated. They carry no pyDeprecate metadata. This preserves check, expiry, and policy results when projects mix both decorators.

Pass include_pep702=True to include these symbols:

Field PEP 702-only value api_type The usual shape, such as callable, class, class method, or staticmethod. pep702_message The decorator's message string, possibly empty. deprecated_info Metadata without versions, because PEP 702 records none. empty_deprecated_in Always True.

Use row.pep702_message is not None to identify these rows. Every pyDeprecate row has pep702_message=None.

Applying schedule filters. Drop PEP 702-only rows before applying your own empty_deprecated_in, expiry, or report filters to an opt-in scan.

A pyDeprecate wrapper with PEP 702 stacked on top remains a regular row with its full schedule. See the static-checker pattern.

from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers
from tests.collections import pep702

rows = find_deprecation_wrappers(pep702, include_pep702=True)
for row in rows:
    if row.pep702_message is not None:
        print(f"{row.function} [{row.api_type}]: {row.pep702_message or '<empty message>'}")
Output: row.function, row.api_type, row.pep702_message 
Pep702CallableClass [class]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Pep702DefaultCategoryClass [class]: Use `Pep702StaticTarget` instead.
Pep702ExplicitHooks [class]: Use `Pep702StaticTarget` instead.
Pep702ExplicitHooks.__init_subclass__ [classmethod]: Do not subclass; use `Pep702StaticTarget`.
Pep702ExplicitHooks.__new__ [staticmethod]: Build through `Pep702StaticTarget` instead.
Pep702ForeignMember.local_old [class method]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Pep702MixedMembers.old_pep702 [class method]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Pep702OnlyClass [class]: Use `Pep702StaticTarget` instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers._old_method [class method]: Use the public method instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers._old_value [class method]: Use the public value instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers.old_method [class method]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers.old_static [staticmethod]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers.old_total [class method]: Compute the total from `value` instead.
Pep702OnlyMembers.old_value [class method]: Read `value` instead.
pep702_empty_message [callable]: <empty message>
pep702_only_function [callable]: Use `pep702_target` instead.
Ownership and duplicate rows

A subclass of a PEP 702-deprecated class is not listed. Neither is a ready-made callable instance of one. Both inherit __deprecated__ through the class and are not themselves deprecated.

A class lists only its own PEP 702 markers. Methods inherited from a library base, such as pydantic's BaseModel, belong to that library. They are not repeated under every subclass.

A class with the default warning category produces one row, not three. Its decorator also installs __new__ and __init_subclass__ with the same message. The class row already covers them.

Symbols imported from another top-level package belong to that dependency. For example, from pydantic.deprecated.tools import parse_obj_as is omitted even with recursive=False. A symbol with unknown __module__ stays listed under its exposing module.

A second binding, such as ShortName = LongName, lists PEP 702 members once. They appear under the class's own name, LongName, even if the alias sorts first. Without such a binding, the first scanned name is used.

pyDeprecate rows remain unchanged for aliased classes. They still appear under each name.

Overloads are invisible at runtime. The scan sees only runtime objects. An individual @overload decorated with PEP 702 is invisible because implementation functions replace overload stubs. Those stubs never become module or class members. Static checkers still flag calls matching that overload.

PEP 702 needs Python

The pydeprecate CLI has no --include-pep702 flag. Its gates evaluate schedule metadata: deprecated_in, remove_in, and a replacement. PEP 702 rows lack this metadata, so list them with the Python API.

docs.title: CLI usage
docs.text:
All audit functions are also available through six CLI subcommands: check, expiry, policy, chains, all, and status.

See the CLI Reference for flags and exit codes. See Enforcing the policy in CI for workflow wiring.

docs.title: Detecting Deprecation Chains
docs.text:
A chain forms when a deprecated wrapper targets another deprecated function. Callers receive two notices, and the intermediate hop adds no value.

validate_deprecation_chains() scans a module or package for chains using metadata alone. It requires no source-code inspection.

Two chain types are reported:

Type Meaning Remedy ChainType.TARGET The target is deprecated: a callable forwarding to another function, or a deprecated object passed as deprecated_instance(target=...). Point directly to the final, non-deprecated replacement. ChainType.STACKED Mappings chain through multiple hops. Compose the mappings. ChainType.STACKED covers these patterns:
  • Callable argument mappings form chains.
  • Multiple @deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, args_mapping=...) decorators are stacked.
  • deprecated_class(attrs_mapping=...) maps a deprecated attribute to another key in the same mapping, such as {"a": "b", "b": "c"}.

The example below shows both bad patterns and the correct direct form:

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated, validate_deprecation_wrapper, void


# NEW API — computes a power with the final exponent spelling
def new_power(base: float, exponent: float = 2) -> float:
    return base**exponent


# DEPRECATED API — `power_v2` replaced by `new_power`
@deprecated(target=new_power, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def power_v2(base: float, exponent: float = 2) -> float:
    void(base, exponent)


# DEPRECATED API — `legacy_power` renames "exp" to "exponent" in the same function
@deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0", args_mapping={"exp": "exponent"})
def legacy_power(base: float, exp: float = 2, exponent: float = 2) -> float:
    return base**exponent


# DEPRECATED API — BAD: targets power_v2 (another deprecated forwarder) — ChainType.TARGET
# SOLUTION: point directly to new_power
@deprecated(target=power_v2, deprecated_in="1.5", remove_in="2.5")
def caller_target_chain(base: float, exponent: float = 2) -> float:  # ❌
    return void(base, exponent)


# DEPRECATED API — BAD: targets legacy_power (target=TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP with arg renaming) — ChainType.STACKED
# Mappings chain: "power" -> "exp" -> "exponent" — must be composed.
# SOLUTION: target=new_power, args_mapping={"power": "exponent"}
@deprecated(target=legacy_power, deprecated_in="1.5", remove_in="2.5", args_mapping={"power": "exp"})
def caller_stacked_chain(base: float, power: float = 2) -> float:  # ❌
    return void(base, power)


# DEPRECATED API — GOOD: `caller_direct` targets `new_power` with the composed mapping
@deprecated(target=new_power, deprecated_in="1.5", remove_in="2.5", args_mapping={"power": "exponent"})
def caller_direct(base: float, power: float = 2) -> float:  # ✅
    return void(base, power)


for func in (caller_target_chain, caller_stacked_chain, caller_direct):
    info = validate_deprecation_wrapper(func)
    print(f"{func.__name__}: {info.chain_type}")
Output: f"{func.__name__}: {info.chain_type}" 
caller_target_chain: ChainType.TARGET
caller_stacked_chain: ChainType.STACKED
caller_direct: None

docs.title: pytest integration for chain detection
docs.text:
Add a test that fails whenever a deprecated function in your package targets another deprecated function. The session-scoped autouse fixture variant prevents the entire suite from running until chains are resolved.

import pytest
from deprecate import validate_deprecation_chains

# normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections import chains as my_package


def test_no_deprecation_chains():
    """Ensure no deprecated function targets another deprecated function."""
    issues = validate_deprecation_chains(my_package)

    if issues:
        lines = [
            f"  - {i.function}: target '{getattr(i.deprecated_info.target, '__name__', repr(i.deprecated_info.target))}' is deprecated"
            for i in issues
        ]
        pytest.fail("Found deprecation chains:\n" + "\n".join(lines))


# Alternative: session-scoped auto-use fixture
@pytest.fixture(scope="session", autouse=True)
def enforce_no_deprecation_chains():
    from tests.collections import chains as my_package

    issues = validate_deprecation_chains(my_package)
    if issues:
        raise AssertionError(f"Found {len(issues)} deprecation chain(s). Fix before running tests.")

Use recursive=False to restrict scanning to the top-level module only, which can speed up large codebases when you know submodules are clean.

docs.title: Detecting Mapping Incompatibilities
docs.text:
deprecated_class(args_mapping=...) remaps deprecated argument names before forwarding to the target constructor.

Positional-only target parameters

A replacement name declared before / is POSITIONAL_ONLY, so Python rejects it as a keyword argument. The proxy detects this at decoration time and emits a UserWarning. At call time, it forwards remapped values positionally.

Construction uses the regular constructor. Required positional-only parameters, frozen dataclasses, and classes deriving state in __post_init__ therefore work correctly.

validate_mapping_compatibility() reports wrappers with a non-empty args_mapping_positional_only field. This advisory finding makes configurations visible for deliberate review. It does not indicate a failure.

docs.title: The problem: POSITIONAL_ONLY remap target
docs.text:
This class uses the / positional-only separator in its constructor:

from deprecate import deprecated_class


# NEW API — uses positional-only coordinates
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x: float = 0.0, y: float = 0.0, /) -> None:  # POSITIONAL_ONLY with defaults
        self.x = x
        self.y = y


# DEPRECATED API — `OldPoint` remaps "px" and "py" to "x" and "y"
OldPoint = deprecated_class(  # warns: UserWarning — px, py target POSITIONAL_ONLY params
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
    args_mapping={"px": "x", "py": "y"},
)(Point)

# Proxy forwards the remapped values positionally: Point(1.0, 2.0)
p = OldPoint(px=1.0, py=2.0)  # warns: FutureWarning
print(p.x, p.y)
Output: p.x, p.y 
1.0 2.0

Supported constructors. Positional forwarding works with required parameters and parameters that have defaults. Immutable classes without a permissive __setattr__ also construct correctly. Constructors can derive state from these values.

The decoration-time UserWarning most commonly appears through dataclass auto-expansion. An attrs_mapping generates args_mapping entries, and a target field name maps to a positional-only constructor parameter.

docs.title: Scanning for incompatible wrappers
docs.text:
from deprecate import validate_mapping_compatibility

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package

issues = validate_mapping_compatibility(my_package)
print(f"Found {len(issues)} wrappers with POSITIONAL_ONLY mapping incompatibilities")

for info in issues:
    print(f"  {info.module}.{info.function}: incompatible keys = {list(info.args_mapping_positional_only)}")
Output: f"Found {len(issues)} wrappers with POSITIONAL_ONLY mapping incompatibilities" 
Found 8 wrappers with POSITIONAL_ONLY mapping incompatibilities
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DepPositionalOnly: incompatible keys = ['old_val']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DepPositionalOnlyDerived: incompatible keys = ['old_val']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DepPositionalOnlyImmutable: incompatible keys = ['old_val']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DepPositionalOnlyMixed: incompatible keys = ['old_x']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.DepPositionalOnlyRequired: incompatible keys = ['old_val']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.PositionalOnlyProxyHolder.LegacyTarget: incompatible keys = ['old_val']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.depr_resize: incompatible keys = ['size_px']
  tests.collections.api_deprecated.core.depr_scaler: incompatible keys = ['quantity']

The function accepts the same module, recursive, and include_members arguments as find_deprecation_wrappers().

Argument Usage module Pass an imported module object or a dotted string path. recursive=False Scan only the top-level module. include_members=False Skip proxies bound as class attributes, such as PositionalOnlyProxyHolder.LegacyTarget above.

CI reporting

A positional-only mapping is not a defect: the wrapper forwards remapped values positionally and works correctly. Expiry and chain findings can indicate defects.

Prefer pydeprecate check for advisory CI reporting. Positional-only mappings produce advisory warnings with exit 0. Only hard configuration errors, such as invalid argument mappings, cause exit 1.

See the CLI Reference for flags and exit codes.

docs.title: Generating Deprecation Tables
docs.text:
generate_deprecation_table() renders discovered wrapper metadata as a Markdown table suitable for embedding in your project documentation. It supports two style= options:

Style Layout "compact" (default) One row per symbol, with a Current Status column: 📢 Deprecation Active, 💥 Past Removal Date, ℹ️ No Removal Target, and the other labels in the table below. "matrix" One column per release, with D (deprecated), R (remove), and D/R (both in the same release) markers.

Equivalent release spellings. Matrix columns combine spellings such as 1.0, v1.0, and 1.0.0 under the shortest spelling when the audit extra is installed. Without packaging, only the v prefix is ignored.

Compact style — one row per symbol with a lifecycle status column:

from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package
from deprecate import generate_deprecation_table

report = generate_deprecation_table(my_package, current_version="1.5", recursive=False)
print(report.splitlines()[1])
Output: report.splitlines()[1] 
| Original API | API Type | New API | Deprecated | Remove | Current Status |

The following selected rows illustrate the rendered table, using my_package as the module label.

Current version: 1.5

Original API API Type New API Deprecated Remove Current Status my_package.CrossGuardOldClass.__init__ class constructor my_package.CrossGuardClassTargetNew v1.0 v2.0 📢 Deprecation Active my_package.DecoratedDataClass dataclass my_package.NewDataClass v0.5 v1.0 💥 Past Removal Date my_package.ServiceCls.old_class_method classmethod — v1.0 v2.0 📢 Deprecation Active my_package.ServiceCls.old_redirect_method class method my_package.ServiceCls.compute v1.0 v2.0 📢 Deprecation Active my_package.depr_func_no_remove_in callable — v1.0 — ℹ️ No Removal Target my_package.depr_func_same_version callable — v2.0 v2.0 🕒 Scheduled Deprecation my_package.depr_pow_args callable my_package.base_pow_args v1.0 v1.3 💥 Past Removal Date my_package.decorated_sum callable my_package.base_sum_kwargs v0.1 v0.5 💥 Past Removal Date

Compact-table status labels, matching DeprecationStatus, and what triggers each:

Status Trigger 🕒 Scheduled Deprecation The current version is below deprecated_in. ℹ️ No Removal Target remove_in is not set. ⚪ Status Unknown remove_in is set but no current version is available. ⚪ Invalid Removal Target remove_in cannot be parsed as a version. 📢 Deprecation Active The current version is below remove_in, in a different base release. ⏰ Removal Imminent The current version is a dev, alpha or beta pre-release of the remove_in base release. 🔔 Remove Before Release The current version is a release candidate (rc) of the remove_in base release. 💥 Past Removal Date The current version is at or above remove_in.

Matrix style gives each release a column with D, R, or D/R lifecycle markers:

from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package
from deprecate import generate_deprecation_table

matrix = generate_deprecation_table(my_package, current_version="1.5", recursive=False, style="matrix")
print(matrix.splitlines()[1])
Output: matrix.splitlines()[1] 
| Original API | API Type | New API | v0.1 | v0.2 | v0.3 | v0.5 | v0.8 | v1.0 | v1.3 | v1.8 | v2.0 |

The following selected rows illustrate the rendered table, using my_package as the module label.

Current version: 1.5

Original API API Type New API v0.1 v0.5 v1.0 v1.3 v2.0 my_package.CrossGuardOldClass.__init__ class constructor my_package.CrossGuardClassTargetNew D R my_package.DecoratedDataClass dataclass my_package.NewDataClass D R my_package.ServiceCls.old_class_method classmethod — D R my_package.ServiceCls.old_redirect_method class method my_package.ServiceCls.compute D R my_package.depr_func_no_remove_in callable — D my_package.depr_func_same_version callable — D/R my_package.depr_pow_args callable my_package.base_pow_args D R my_package.decorated_sum callable my_package.base_sum_kwargs D R

The table derives all data from __deprecation_config__ decorator metadata so it stays in sync with the code automatically. Install the audit extra (pip install pyDeprecate[audit]) to enable lifecycle status evaluation.

docs.title: pytest integration
docs.text:
Add a test that fails the suite when any deprecated wrapper has an invalid configuration. Wrong argument names are hard errors; identity mappings are worth a warning.

import warnings

import pytest
from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package


def test_deprecated_wrappers_are_valid():
    """Validate all deprecated wrappers have proper configuration."""
    results = find_deprecation_wrappers(my_package)

    # Collect hard configuration errors; identity mappings are worth a warning
    wrong_args = [r for r in results if r.invalid_args or r.misconfigured_target or r.inner_order_property]
    identity_mappings = [r for r in results if r.identity_args_mapping]

    # Raise errors for wrong arguments (critical issues)
    if wrong_args:
        for r in wrong_args:
            print(
                f"ERROR: {r.module}.{r.function}: invalid_args={r.invalid_args}, "
                f"misconfigured_target={r.misconfigured_target}, inner_order_property={r.inner_order_property}"
            )
        pytest.fail(f"Found {len(wrong_args)} deprecated wrappers with invalid configuration")

    # Warn for identity mappings (less severe)
    for r in identity_mappings:
        warnings.warn(f"{r.function} has identity mapping", UserWarning)

docs.title: Enforcing the policy in CI
docs.text:
Use your project's release convention rather than assuming the policy defaults fit.

  1. Set the release numbers in [tool.pydeprecate.policy].
  2. Install your project and pyDeprecate[audit] in CI.
  3. Run the CLI as its own CI step (since v0.16):

The table is the single source of truth. The CLI step enforces it without test code to maintain.

# audit everything in one scan; reads [tool.pydeprecate.policy] and exits 1 on a violation too
pydeprecate all --gate=policy src/mypackage

Policy gate defaults

Without --gate=policy, pydeprecate all prints policy violations as [WARNING] without failing. Set gate = ["policy"] in [tool.pydeprecate] to make policy enforcement the project default.

Before v0.16, run pydeprecate all and a separate pydeprecate policy src/mypackage step.

A one-off override needs no config edit. pydeprecate policy src/mypackage --min-grace=0.3 overrides the table for that run only.

On GitHub Actions, use the ready-made GitHub Action step for the same gate.

docs.title: Monorepo: several packages in one run
docs.text:
Pass every package to one command: pydeprecate all --gate=policy packages/core/src/core packages/cli/src/cli (since v0.16).

  • Each package uses its own [tool.pydeprecate] settings.
  • Each package uses the version from its nearest pyproject.toml.
  • Findings appear in one set of sections.
  • Each package has a table under a ### <package> heading.
  • One exit code covers all packages.

Paths are checked before imports. A typo or broken pyproject.toml in any package fails the run with exit 2 before scanning. A missing submodule of an importable package, such as pkg.nosuch, is found only when its path is reached.

Process and import isolation. Packages sharing the same top-level import name need separate runs. Multiple paths remaining after deduplication use separate Python workers for import-mode scans. A shared import may initialize once in each worker.

One retained path runs in the calling process. --static reads source without importing packages or starting workers. See Several paths in one run.

docs.title: Pre-commit Integration
docs.text:
A pre-commit hook gives local feedback before you push, without running tests or waiting for CI.

Choose an import environment

The scan imports your package to read wrappers. Your package and its runtime dependencies must be importable in the hook's environment. This determines which recipe fits.

docs.title: Local hook
docs.text:
Use a local hook in your development environment when your package has runtime dependencies.

Install pip install 'pyDeprecate[audit]' in the same environment as your tests. The hook uses that environment's pydeprecate CLI, so every submodule imports as it does at runtime:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: pydeprecate
        name: pydeprecate
        entry: pydeprecate check # add the package path if it is not under src/
        language: system # spelled `unsupported` since pre-commit 4.4; `system` still works
        pass_filenames: false # the CLI scans packages, not individual files
        types: [python] # runs only when a Python file is staged
        require_serial: true

ci:
  skip: [pydeprecate] # pre-commit.ci has no project environment to import from

docs.title: Import-mode remote hook
docs.text:
For packages without third-party import dependencies, use the repository's hook manifest (since v0.15.0):

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/Borda/pyDeprecate
    rev: v0.15.0 # the first tag shipping the hook
    hooks:
      - id: pydeprecate-check # finds the package under src/; add `args: [mypkg]` for any other location

pre-commit installs the hook into an isolated environment. It contains pyDeprecate and CLI dependencies, but none of your package's runtime dependencies.

Replacing hook dependencies

additional_dependencies replaces the hook's own dependency list. Start with "pyDeprecate[audit]", then append your package's runtime dependencies. pip resolves that entry to the hook's own checkout, including its audit extra.

Omitting that entry leaves pydeprecate without packaging, which expiry and any policy version comparison need. Python 3.9–3.10 also cannot read [tool.pydeprecate] from pyproject.toml.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/Borda/pyDeprecate
    rev: v0.15.0
    hooks:
      - id: pydeprecate-check
        additional_dependencies: ["pyDeprecate[audit]", numpy, requests] # the hook's own entry first, then your package's runtime dependencies

A missing dependency can pass silently

A failed submodule import emits UserWarning: audit: skipped <module>. The scan skips that module and continues. See Troubleshooting.

pre-commit hides output from passing hooks. A missing dependency can therefore leave modules unaudited without a visible failure.

Prefer the local hook when your package has runtime dependencies. Pin rev to the pyDeprecate release your project depends on.

docs.title: Import-free remote hooks
docs.text:
pydeprecate-expiry-static and pydeprecate-policy-static read source with ast without importing your package. They need none of its runtime dependencies.

Release availability. These hooks ship with v0.16.0, the upcoming release, not yet tagged. The following recipe fails until that release is published.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/Borda/pyDeprecate
    rev: v0.16.0 # the first tag shipping the static hooks
    hooks:
      - id: pydeprecate-expiry-static
      - id: pydeprecate-policy-static

The static hooks check removal deadlines and policy rules for recognized wrappers with resolvable relevant settings.

Static coverage is incomplete. Recognized unresolved forms emit a not statically resolvable gap without failing the hook. Some forms remain invisible without a gap.

Read output with pre-commit run --verbose when first enabling a hook. Use an import-mode audit for fuller coverage. See Static mode.

Configuration checks and chains require imported wrappers. Keep pydeprecate check in a local hook or CI.

Hook trust boundary

Both local hooks and import-mode remote hooks import your package. Import-time code runs with your user's permissions.

Run untrusted checkouts, including fork pull requests in CI, without secrets or privileged credentials. An isolated dependency environment does not make that code trustworthy.

Run a configured hook on demand using its ID:

Recipe Hook ID Local. pydeprecate Import-mode remote. pydeprecate-check Static remote expiry. pydeprecate-expiry-static Static remote policy. pydeprecate-policy-static

The following commands use the local ID:

# Get a clear signal before pushing (runs when a Python file is staged):
pre-commit run pydeprecate

# Or check regardless of what is staged:
pre-commit run pydeprecate --all-files

docs.title: Hook scope and configuration
docs.text:
The hook ignores staged filenames and scans the whole package each time. Import-mode discovery resolves wrappers through importable modules, never individual files.

Repository layout Default discovery without a path in args One package under src/. Audit that package. No args is needed. Otherwise, one package at the repository root. Audit that package. No args is needed. Two or more root packages, such as mypkg/ and tests/. Fail with a non-zero exit and contains multiple packages (mypkg, tests), rather than passing an empty scan.

Name the package explicitly for multiple-package roots, such as args: [mypkg].

Each hook already includes its subcommand in entry:

Hook ID Command pydeprecate-check, or its alias pydeprecate Run check. pydeprecate-policy Run policy. pydeprecate-expiry Run expiry. pydeprecate-chains Run chains. pydeprecate-all Run all. pydeprecate-expiry-static Run import-free expiry: the same scan as args: [--static] on pydeprecate-expiry, but also verbose and run on TOML changes. pydeprecate-policy-static Run import-free policy: the same scan as args: [--static] on pydeprecate-policy, but also verbose and run on TOML changes.

See Static mode for import-free scanning.

  • Pass flags and the package path through args, in any order.
  • Use args: [--exit-zero] to report without blocking while clearing a backlog.
  • Use one pydeprecate-all hook with args: [--gate=policy] to gate on policy too (since v0.16).
  • This replaces a second pydeprecate-policy hook with one scan and one import of your package.
  • List several packages in args to audit them in one run (since v0.16).

Changes to project configuration

Static hooks run for Python and pyproject.toml changes. Every subcommand reads [tool.pydeprecate]. expiry and all also read the project version from pyproject.toml.

For import-mode hooks to run on pyproject.toml-only changes, override both filters:

types: [file]
files: '(\.py|(^|/)pyproject\.toml)$'

Otherwise, the manifest's types: [python] remains active. pre-commit requires a file to match every filter. A pyproject.toml-only commit would skip the hook.

docs.title: CLI commands and exit codes
docs.text:
The CLI provides six subcommands. These choices cover common integration needs:

Command Use check Validate wrapper configuration. policy Enforce your project's deprecation governance rules. all Run every check in one pass and append a deprecation table. status Generate a standalone Markdown deprecation table without checks.

See the CLI Reference for every flag and exit code.

# Install CLI + audit extras (audit needed for expiry checks)
pip install 'pyDeprecate[audit]'

# check — exits 1 on invalid arg mappings, misconfigured targets or inner-order properties
pydeprecate check src/your_package

# all — exits 1 on any check error, chains, or expired wrappers; appends deprecation table
# policy violations are printed here but change this exit code only with --gate=policy (since v0.16)
pydeprecate all src/your_package
pydeprecate all --gate=policy src/your_package

# several packages in one run, one exit code (since v0.16)
pydeprecate all src/pkg_a src/pkg_b

# policy — exits 1 if any deprecation breaks a governance rule
pydeprecate policy src/your_package

# status — standalone deprecation status table only (no checks, not a pass/fail gate)
pydeprecate status src/your_package

# Advisory-only: findings exit 0 instead of 1; usage (2) and scan/internal (3) errors still fail
pydeprecate check src/your_package --exit-zero

Exit codes (see CLI Reference — Exit codes for per-subcommand details):

Exit code Meaning 0 No hard errors (or --exit-zero was set) 1 Hard error found: invalid arg mappings, chains, expired wrappers, or policy violations under policy or all --gate=policy; with --strict, also any gap 2 A malformed setting: --exclude, strict, gate, or for policy a rule value, from a flag or from [tool.pydeprecate]; a typed --strict with --exit-zero 3 The audit did not run: the scanned package cannot be imported, or an internal CLI error

--exit-zero turns exit 1 into 0 and never masks 2 or 3.

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text:
pyDeprecate ships a composite GitHub Action that runs the CLI as one workflow step (since v0.15.0). It uses the job's own Python, like a local pre-commit hook.

The scan imports your package from the checkout, so the package itself needs no installation. Every module's runtime dependencies must still be importable.

  1. Set up Python.
  2. Install the runtime dependencies. Installing the project is the simplest approach.
  3. Add the action step:
# .github/workflows/deprecations.yml
name: Deprecations
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - run: pip install -e . # pulls in the runtime dependencies the scanned modules import

      - name: Audit deprecations and enforce the policy
        uses: Borda/pyDeprecate@v0.16.0 # pin a release tag or a commit SHA
        with:
          path: src/mypackage
          args: --gate=policy # policy violations fail the step too, from the same scan
          summary: true # add a deprecation status table to the job summary

A monorepo lists one path per line (since v0.16). Each package uses its own settings, and one exit code covers the scan:

- uses: Borda/pyDeprecate@v0.16.0
  with:
    path: |
      packages/core/src/core
      packages/cli/src/cli
    args: --gate=policy

With v0.15.0, which has no --gate, run the policy as a second step: subcommand: policy with install: false.

Input Default Meaning subcommand all One of check, expiry, policy, chains, all, status; any other value fails the step with exit code 2. path empty Package directory or importable module name, relative to the workspace; several, one per line, are scanned in one run (since v0.16; empty lines are dropped). Empty lets the CLI pick the single package under src/, else the single package at the repository root. A path starting with - fails the step with exit code 2; write such a directory as ./-name and pass CLI options through args. args empty Extra CLI flags, split with shell-style quoting, e.g. --exclude='mypackage.tests,*._legacy*' --version 2.0. Backslashes are escape characters, so quote Windows paths or use /. fail-on-gap false Fail the step when any part of the audit did not run (--strict, since v0.16), such as a module that could not be imported; not valid with exit-zero or status; exit-zero: true also switches off a strict = true from pyproject.toml, so an advisory step passes. With install: false and an older pyDeprecate the CLI rejects the option with exit code 2. exit-zero false Report findings without failing the step (--exit-zero); not valid with status. install true Install pyDeprecate[audit] from the action's own ref into the job's Python. summary false Append the markdown deprecation status table of the gate's own scan to the job summary, read from the report the CLI writes with --report-json, so it covers exactly what the gate scanned however path and args name the package. Summary failures only warn and preserve the gate result. No summary on CLI exit 2 or 3. sarif false Also write the findings as a SARIF 2.1.0 file (--report-sarif, since v0.16) and publish its path as the sarif-file output; not valid with status.

The step returns the CLI's exit code. Exit 3 also produces an error annotation identifying a scan or internal error.

Action-specific failures. These conditions behave as follows:

Condition Exit behavior A path starts with -. Exit 2. pip install fails with install: true. Return pip's exit code. The CLI process cannot start. Return 1. args holds --, -h/--help, or a --report-json or --report-sarif option; use the report-json output to keep a report. Exit 2. A boolean input is not true, false, 1 or 0. Exit 2. exit-zero, fail-on-gap or sarif is combined with status, or fail-on-gap with exit-zero. Exit 2.

Static and advisory runs. The action has no static input. Pass --static through args with subcommand: expiry or policy. See Static mode.

A failing run adds an error annotation to the pull request's checks. The CLI has no "fail on warning" mode. Advisory findings, such as identity mappings, never fail the step.

Set exit-zero: true to report hard errors without blocking while clearing a backlog. Set fail-on-gap: true to fail on incomplete audits. Every gap the run annotates then also fails it.

Findings become annotations on their wrapper's line:

  1. Annotate errors first, then warnings, within GitHub's limit of 10 annotations per level for one step. Gaps and the gate's own exited 1 error use some of those slots first, so a few fewer findings are shown.
  2. Add one notice counting the remaining findings.

Annotation limits and accepted findings. The log and report retain every finding. Findings accepted through --ignore or --baseline are never annotated. Gaps keep one warning per kind.

The step publishes outputs for later steps; give it an id to read them:

Output Value exit-code The step's exit code; always set. findings, errors, warnings, gaps, suppressed Counts from the run's report; empty when the CLI wrote no report (exit 2 or 3, or an older CLI kept with install: false). report-json Path of a copy of the run's --report-json file, kept in RUNNER_TEMP until the job ends. sarif-file Path of the SARIF file when sarif: true; empty otherwise.

SARIF is GitHub code scanning's input format. Uploading it creates alerts on wrapper lines, beyond the failed job.

  1. Set sarif: true on the audit action.
  2. Upload its findings with upload-sarif, even when the gate fails.

Code scanning permissions

Uploads fail with a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN. Give the job security-events: write and retain contents: read for checkout. Private repositories also need actions: read.

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write
  actions: read  # required for private repositories

- uses: Borda/pyDeprecate@v0.16.0
  id: pydeprecate
  with:
    subcommand: all
    sarif: true
- uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
  if: always() && steps.pydeprecate.outputs.sarif-file != ''
  with:
    sarif_file: ${{ steps.pydeprecate.outputs.sarif-file }}

The action ref pins the installed version. With install: true (the default), the action installs pyDeprecate from its own commit. Thus, @v0.15.0 audits with 0.15.0.

This replaces the job's existing pyDeprecate version for every later step. The action warns when it replaces a version.

Pin the action to your project's pyDeprecate release. Alternatively, install pyDeprecate[audit] yourself and set install: false.

Also set install: false where pip is unavailable, such as a uv-managed virtual environment.

A green run can still have gaps. A failed submodule import is skipped with UserWarning: audit: skipped <module>. expiry, including inside all, skips removal deadlines when the package version cannot be detected. Both cases can still pass.

The action reads gaps from the CLI's --report-json report, even when the package silences warnings. It creates one warning annotation per gap kind. Check annotations whenever package installation changes.

Pass args: --version 2.0 when neither the installed package nor pyproject.toml provides a detectable version.

Import-time code runs with job permissions

The action imports your package and executes its import-time code, exactly like the CLI. Never use pull_request_target with a checkout of the pull request's head. Untrusted code would receive the base repository's secrets and write token.

Workflow commands printed during the scan are ignored only while the CLI runs. Descendant-process output after the CLI exits is not fenced by stop-commands.

This is not a sandbox. Imported code runs in the job environment and can write the files behind GITHUB_ENV, GITHUB_PATH, and GITHUB_OUTPUT.
