docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: The pydeprecate CLI runs all four audit checks directly from the command line, without writing a Python script. These checks cover wrapper configuration, expiry enforcement, policy linting, and chain detection.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install 'pyDeprecate[audit]'

Start with [audit] unless you are certain you will never use expiry, policy, or all. The [audit] extra pulls in packaging.

Check When it needs packaging expiry It always requires packaging. policy, including the policy phase of all It needs packaging only when a wrapper's deprecated_in/remove_in is actually compared against a version. A policy scan with no version fields set never imports it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pydeprecate all src/mypackage   # run all checks + deprecation table in one pass
pydeprecate check path/to/your/package   # validate wrapper config
pydeprecate check mypackage.submodule    # importable module name also accepted
pydeprecate policy src/mypackage         # gate on your deprecation-governance rules
pydeprecate all --gate=policy src/pkg_a src/pkg_b   # several packages, policy gated too, one scan each (since v0.16)

Quick demo using pyDeprecate's own test fixtures (no package setup needed):

# Run all checks + deprecation table on the bundled test fixtures
pydeprecate all tests --version 1.2
# Standalone deprecation status table only
pydeprecate status tests --version 1.2

tests/ contains pyDeprecate's own deprecation fixtures. Every subcommand scans a path the same way. It accepts a package directory, a plain directory of top-level modules, or an importable module name; see Path formats.

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text:
checkexpirypolicychainsallstatus

This subcommand validates wrapper configuration: invalid args_mapping keys, identity mappings, no-effect wrappers, and deprecated-to-deprecated chains. It is backed by find_deprecation_wrappers().

pydeprecate check path/to/your/package
pydeprecate check mypackage.submodule
Finding Exit code Invalid argument mappings The command exits 1. Misconfigured targets The command exits 1 for target=False, TargetMode.NOTIFY with an ignored args_mapping, attrs_mapping or args_extra, TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP without an args_mapping or with an extra attrs_mapping, or deprecated_class(target=TargetMode.ATTRS_REMAP) without an attrs_mapping or with an ignored args_mapping or args_extra. Inner-order @property @deprecated wrappers The command exits 1; only the getter warns, leaving the setter and deleter unprotected. Chains, identity mappings, no-effect wrappers and positional-only mappings These are reported as warnings; the command exits 0.

Chains in all

check treats chains as advisory warnings (exit 0). all treats chains as hard errors (exit 1), because all ≡ check + expiry + policy + chains. The chains check exits 1 on any chain found.

policy remains advisory inside all unless you pass --gate=policy.

This subcommand checks whether any deprecated wrappers have passed their remove_in deadline using validate_deprecation_expiry(). It requires the [audit] extra.

# explicit version
pydeprecate expiry path/to/your/package --version 2.0.0

# auto-detect version (pyproject.toml, installed metadata, then package __version__)
pydeprecate expiry path/to/your/package

The command exits 1 if any wrapper is past its removal deadline. Use --exit-zero to suppress exit 1 when expired wrappers are found.

Missing packaging skips expiry. If packaging is not installed, the check is skipped with a warning. It exits 0, or exit 1 under strict mode.

This subcommand checks whether each deprecation was scheduled responsibly, using validate_deprecation_policy(). Every violation message is prefixed with the slug of the rule it broke. policy never needs a package version, so it takes no --version flag.

Rule Default Dependency min-grace The rule is on. It requires the [audit] extra. message-required The rule is on. It works without the extra. 
# default policy: three-minor grace window on a clean release boundary, guidance required
pydeprecate policy path/to/your/package

# tune the window to your own release convention — here: removals only at a major
pydeprecate policy path/to/your/package --min-grace=1.0

# switch individual rules off
pydeprecate policy path/to/your/package --min-grace=None --message-required=False
Outcome Exit code Any enabled rule finds a violation The command exits 1. --min-grace is malformed The command exits 2. The nearest pyproject.toml cannot be read or parsed The command exits 2 and prints Cannot read <path>: <err>. The scan is clean, or --exit-zero is passed The command exits 0.

Missing packaging skips only min-grace. If packaging is not installed, min-grace is skipped with a warning. message-required still runs and can return exit 1.

Advisory policy in all

The policy defaults encode a project convention: a three-minor grace window on a clean release boundary. Not every repository shares that convention, so pydeprecate all runs this check in advisory mode by default. Violations are printed but never change all's exit code.

Inside all, the violation table renders as [WARNING] (yellow). Its trailer notes "advisory here — run pydeprecate policy to gate on it".

To gate CI on the policy, pass --gate=policy to all (since v0.16), or set gate = ["policy"] in [tool.pydeprecate]. Violations then render as [ERROR] without the trailer and fail the run, from the same single scan. The dedicated pydeprecate policy subcommand gates on them too.

A config-read failure is the one exception to "advisory". An unreadable or malformed pyproject.toml still exits 2 inside all too, before the chains check ever runs; see below.

This subcommand detects two kinds of chains using validate_deprecation_chains():

  • ChainType.TARGET identifies wrappers whose target is itself a deprecated callable.
  • ChainType.STACKED identifies stacked argument mappings that should be collapsed.
pydeprecate chains path/to/your/package

The command exits 1 if any chains are found.

This subcommand runs all four checks in a single scan pass, then appends a compact markdown deprecation table:

  • find_deprecation_wrappers() validates wrapper configuration.
  • validate_deprecation_expiry() enforces removal deadlines.
  • validate_deprecation_policy() checks policy.
  • validate_deprecation_chains() detects chains.

Missing packaging leaves some checks running. If packaging is not installed, expiry and policy's min-grace rule are skipped with a warning. message-required still runs, and the other checks continue.

# explicit version
pydeprecate all path/to/your/package --version 2.0.0

# auto-detect version
pydeprecate all path/to/your/package

# also save the appended table
pydeprecate all path/to/your/package --output DEPRECATIONS.md

# also gate on the policy, from the same scan (since v0.16)
pydeprecate all path/to/your/package --gate=policy

The command exits 1 if any hard error is found. Hard errors include invalid argument mappings, misconfigured targets, inner-order properties, deprecated-to-deprecated chains, or expired wrappers. The deprecation table is always appended regardless of pass/fail outcome.

Policy violations are advisory here by default, because the defaults encode a project convention that not every repository shares. They render as [WARNING] with a trailer noting the check is advisory and naming pydeprecate policy as the gate. They never contribute to the exit code.

--gate=policy (since v0.16) makes them errors that fail all exactly as pydeprecate policy would. --gate takes a comma-separated list of check, expiry, policy and chains, and only adds checks. check, expiry and chains always gate, so today only policy changes anything.

Configuration failures

Advisory treatment covers violation counts only. A policy configuration failure still exits 2, printing Cannot read <path>: <err>, before the chains check ever runs. This includes an unreadable or unparsable nearest pyproject.toml, or a malformed [tool.pydeprecate.policy] value.

Dependency state Behaviour packaging is missing Expiry is skipped and policy skips min-grace, but its packaging-free message-required rule still runs. Without --gate=policy, that rule is advisory, so neither affects all's exit 1. With --gate=policy, a message-required violation still exits 1 unless --exit-zero applies. packaging is missing and explicit --version is malformed The malformed version is also advisory. packaging is available An invalid explicit --version exits 2.

This subcommand generates and prints a markdown deprecation table to stdout. It runs no checks and exits 0 on success; an invalid --style or --version exits 2. Use this when you only want to render the deprecation status table without running any validation.

pydeprecate status path/to/your/package
pydeprecate status path/to/your/package --style matrix
pydeprecate status path/to/your/package --version 2.0.0 --output DEPRECATIONS.md
Style Layout --style compact (default) It renders one row per symbol with a status column. --style matrix It renders one column per release with D, R and D/R lifecycle markers. D/R means deprecated and removed in the same release.

Equivalent release spellings. With the audit extra installed, spellings of one release such as 1.0, v1.0 and 1.0.0 share a column. Without packaging, only spellings that differ by the v prefix merge.

--output FILE writes the table to a file in addition to printing it to stdout.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Default check expiry policy chains all status Effect Note --version VERSION auto-detected ✓ ✓ ✓ Package version for deadline comparison, applied to every path. Auto-detected per path if omitted (see below). policy compares deprecated_in to remove_in only, so it takes no version. --gate CHECKS pyproject.toml ✓ Checks all gates on beyond check, expiry and chains, comma-separated: --gate=policy makes policy violations errors that fail the run. Since v0.16. Default is gate of [tool.pydeprecate], else none; --gate= switches the file's list off. Unknown check → exit 2. --no-recursive off ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Scan top-level module only; skip submodules. Also spelled --recursive=false. --no-include-members off ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Leave deprecated class members (methods, constructors, descriptors) out of the scan; only module-level wrappers are checked. Members are scanned by default, as by every audit function (include_members=True). Also spelled --include-members=false. --exit-zero off ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Exit 0 instead of 1 when hard errors are found — useful for advisory CI steps; usage errors (2) and scan or internal errors (3) still fail. --strict pyproject.toml ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Exit 1 when any part of the audit did not run, even with no finding. This means any pydeprecate gap: line, such as an unimportable module or an unresolved version. Since v0.16. The default is strict of [tool.pydeprecate], else off; --no-strict switches it off for one run. A typed --strict together with --exit-zero → exit 2. A typed --exit-zero overrides a strict = true that only pyproject.toml sets; one stderr note states the run is not strict. --ignore PATTERNS pyproject.toml ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Accept known findings without fixing them: entries module:symbol (every rule) or rule:module:symbol (one rule, or *), each part an fnmatch glob; comma-separated and repeatable. Suppressed findings are not printed, counted or gated on. Since v0.16. Default is ignore of [tool.pydeprecate], else nothing; --ignore= switches the file's list off. Malformed entry → exit 2. --baseline FILE pyproject.toml ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Accept every finding listed in an earlier --report-json file (since pyDeprecate v0.16), matched by finding id. Since v0.16. Default is baseline of [tool.pydeprecate], relative to that file; --baseline= switches it off. A file that is missing or unreadable, or is not a report with a findings list → exit 2. --exclude pyproject.toml ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Glob patterns over full dotted module names to leave out of the scan; the scan itself never imports a matching package nor descends into it. One pattern, or comma-separated. Default is the exclude list of [tool.pydeprecate] (see below), else nothing. Quote the value — an unquoted * is expanded by the shell first. Malformed → exit 2. --style compact ✓ Table rendering style — compact (default) or matrix. --output FILE stdout only ✓ ✓ Also save the markdown table to a file. Table is always printed to stdout regardless. For all, a failure to write the file is reported but never changes the exit code. --report-json FILE off ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Write the run's machine-readable record for CI tooling: the deprecation table of this run's scan, every gap and every finding (see below). Written on exit 0 or 1 only; a write failure is reported on stderr and never changes the exit code. --report-sarif FILE off ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Write the run's active findings as a SARIF 2.1.0 file for code-scanning tools (see below). Since v0.16. Written on exit 0 or 1 only; a write failure is reported on stderr and never changes the exit code. --static off ✓ ✓ Read the package's source with ast instead of importing it, for an environment without its runtime dependencies (see Static mode). Nothing from the package is imported or run. A wrapper the source alone does not settle is a not statically resolvable gap, not a finding.

A bare pydeprecate policy src/mypackage runs a recursive scan and exits 1 on violations. It applies both default-on rules below: --min-grace=0.3 and --message-required=True. The project's pyproject.toml can override these defaults; see Project configuration in pyproject.toml.

Flags and the path may come in any order. pydeprecate check --exit-zero src/mypackage scans src/mypackage, using the order a pre-commit hook produces from its args.

Syntax Behaviour Boolean flags They accept true, false, 1 or 0, case-insensitively, as --flag value or --flag=value. Negated booleans Use --no-flag, as in --no-recursive. The older --noflag spelling (--norecursive) still works but is not listed in --help. Option names Every option may use dashes or underscores (--exit-zero, --exit_zero), but never abbreviations. Option values Values stay strings, so --version 0.10 and --min-grace=0.10 keep their trailing zero. Positional arguments Every positional argument is a path; see Several paths in one run. Invalid syntax A short flag such as -r src/mypackage, or a boolean value other than true/false/1/0, exits 2. The command does not scan something you did not name. Subcommand help pydeprecate <subcommand> --help lists the options of each subcommand.

docs.title: Several paths in one run
docs.text:
Since v0.16 every subcommand takes several paths — pydeprecate all src/pkg_a src/pkg_b — and audits them in one run with one exit code:

  1. Every path is checked before anything is imported.
  2. Duplicate and recursively covered paths are combined when their settings and versions allow it.
  3. The retained paths are scanned one after another, each with its own import root, settings, and auto-detected version.
  4. The console prints one scan header per path, then each check's findings of all paths in one section. For all and status, it then prints one table per path under a ### <package> heading.
  5. One exit code covers all paths. Each path is judged with its own strict mode and --gate list; the run fails when any path fails.

docs.title: Path validation
docs.text:
The following conditions exit 2 with nothing scanned:

  • A path is a file or a directory of several packages.
  • A name is neither an existing path nor a findable module.
  • Any path's pyproject.toml contains a malformed setting.
  • Two paths import as the same top-level name from different places. The diagnostic is <a> and <b> both import as <name>; scan them in separate runs.

A plain directory takes part in import-name checks with the bare name of each top-level file it scans. A file its exclude leaves out takes no part.

Missing submodules are found later. Validation looks up only the top-level package without importing it. A missing submodule of an importable package (pkg.nosuch) therefore exits 2 when its path is scanned, after the paths before it. No report is written.

docs.title: Duplicate and covered paths
docs.text:
Paths Scan behaviour The same path is given twice It is scanned once, with one stderr note. A package and a subpackage its recursive scan imports They are scanned once, with one stderr note. Every directory between them must hold an __init__.py, and the package's exclude must not leave the subpackage out. Any other subpackage It keeps its own scan. A covered path finds a different [tool.pydeprecate] file It exits 2, since those settings would be dropped. Scan it in a separate run. A covered path finds its own version during auto-detection It exits 2, since that version would be dropped. Scan it in a separate run. A covered path finds neither its own settings nor version It takes the covering path's settings and version. For example, src/pkg/sub has only a repository-root pyproject.toml.

Version auto-detection applies to expiry, all and status without --version. A covered path's own version can come from a nearer pyproject.toml with a [project] table. For a dotted module name such as pkg.component, it can come from an installed pkg-component distribution.

docs.title: Scan settings and workers
docs.text:
Each path takes its [tool.pydeprecate] settings from the pyproject.toml nearest to that path. These settings are exclude, strict, ignore, baseline, gate and the policy rules.

Retained paths and mode Execution More than one path, import mode Each scan runs in a fresh Python worker process. A shared dependency can therefore initialize once in each worker. Live parent-process monkeypatches, custom import finders and sys.modules state are not inherited. One path, import mode The scan runs in the calling process. --static The scan reads source without importing it or starting these workers.

A typed --version applies to every path, and the run says so before the first scan header. Flags apply to every path.

Run-wide exit handling. --exit-zero applies to the whole run. It conflicts with a typed --strict, but overrides strict mode configured in any path’s pyproject.toml.

The report holds every path in paths, versions, and each finding's and gap's path. The SARIF file lists them in run.properties.paths and gives each result its path.

Legacy positional versions

With exactly two positionals, expiry, all and status can still read the second one as the version. It must name no existing path or findable module and parse as a version, as in pydeprecate expiry src/mypackage 2.0.

This form is deprecated and stops working in v1.0. The run prints a notice on stderr asking for --version instead.

A second positional that is not a version is a second path. A mistyped one is therefore reported as No such path or importable module.

Operands after a -- separator are always paths. pydeprecate expiry -- src/mypackage 2.0 scans 2.0 as a second path instead of reading it as the version. Pass --version 2.0 there.

docs.title: Audit gaps
docs.text:
Passing runs can have gaps

A run can pass without auditing everything. A gap leaves the exit code alone unless strict mode is on; see Exit codes.

Each gap is reported as one unwrapped stderr line starting with pydeprecate gap: <kind>:. These lines stay visible in a CI log.

Kind Meaning or reporting detail module not audited One line is printed per submodule that failed to import, whatever warnings filters the audited package installs. One additional <package>.* line appears when a recursive walk stopped early and left remaining submodules unaudited. version not resolved The version was not resolved. version not PEP 440 The version is not PEP 440. remove_in not PEP 440 A wrapper's own remove_in is not a valid PEP 440 version. Its removal deadline (expiry) or grace window (policy's min-grace) was skipped. One line is printed per wrapper; all names each wrapper once. deprecated_in not PEP 440 A wrapper's own deprecated_in is not a valid PEP 440 version, so policy's min-grace skipped its grace window. One line is printed per wrapper. epoch change A forward change of PEP 440 epoch makes the min-grace window unmeasurable. One line is printed per wrapper. packaging missing packaging is missing. nested files not audited Nested files were not audited. other copy audited The scanned package's import name was already taken by a copy from another directory, so that copy was audited. It may be the CLI's own deprecate, or an editable install of another checkout. Run the scan in the checkout's own environment. not statically resolvable A --static run could not read a wrapper, or a setting one of its rules needs, from the source alone. See Static mode.

docs.title: JSON report
docs.text:
For tooling, --report-json FILE records the same run as JSON — every subcommand takes it. The file has layout version (schema) 1; since v0.16 it also holds one record per finding:

{
  "schema": 1,
  "tool": { "name": "pyDeprecate", "version": "0.16.0" },
  "command": "expiry",
  "mode": "import",
  "paths": ["src/mypackage"],
  "versions": [{ "path": "src/mypackage", "package": "mypackage", "value": "2.0", "source": "user-provided" }],
  "options": { "strict": false, "exit_zero": false, "gates": ["expiry"], "recursive": true, "exclude": [] },
  "gate": { "failed": true, "reasons": ["findings"] },
  "exit_code": 1,
  "table": "| API | ... |",
  "gaps": [
    {
      "kind": "module not audited",
      "detail": "mypackage.extra: ImportError(...)",
      "hint": "install the scanned package's runtime dependencies in the environment that runs the scan",
      "path": "src/mypackage"
    }
  ],
  "findings": [
    {
      "id": "expired:mypackage:old_fn",
      "rule": "expired",
      "check": "expiry",
      "level": "error",
      "message": "Callable `mypackage.old_fn` was scheduled for removal in version 1.5 but still exists in version 2.0. ...",
      "details": [],
      "subject": { "module": "mypackage", "symbol": "old_fn", "api_type": "callable", "label": "Callable `mypackage.old_fn`" },
      "deprecated_in": "1.0",
      "remove_in": "1.5",
      "location": { "file": "src/mypackage/__init__.py", "line": 8 },
      "path": "src/mypackage"
    }
  ],
  "suppressed": [],
  "summary": { "findings": 1, "errors": 1, "warnings": 0, "notes": 0, "gaps": 1, "suppressed": 0, "baseline_unmatched": 0, "ignore_unmatched": 0 }
}
Field Meaning mode It is static for a --static run and import otherwise. table It is the markdown deprecation table of the scan that ran, or null when it could not be rendered. Several paths join one table per path, each under a ### <package> heading. A note replaces any table that could not be rendered. Each gap It carries one of the kinds above, its detail, a remedy and the scan path it came from. paths and versions They list every scanned path. options It summarises the run. strict is true when any path is strict; gates and exclude are the union over the paths. findings It lists every finding the subcommand evaluates, once per id at its level in this run, sorted by level and then id. error fails the gate; warning is reported only. message It is the finding's full description. location It identifies where the wrapper is defined. The POSIX path is relative to the repository root when the file is under it, else absolute. This is the same root as the SARIF locations below. Location line The line is that of the wrapper's first decorator. Null locations line is null for a deprecated module. location is null for a deprecated_instance data object or a class built at runtime. Static locations A --static run places a wrapper as an import run does when the source shows its definition. A wrapper of an object defined in another module or bound more than once has no location there. gate It says whether the gate failed before --exit-zero and why: findings, and gaps under --strict. exit_code It is the process exit code.

The id is <rule>:<module>:<symbol>. A deprecated module has an empty symbol: expired:mypackage.oldmod:. The id holds no version, line, message or path.

It survives moved code, a version bump and reworded messages. It changes only when the symbol, its module or the rule is renamed.

Naming case Effect on the id A wrapper has several public names It is reported under the one named like the wrapper (__name__), so adding an alias does not rename its id. Its __name__ is private (old = deprecated(...)(_impl)), or it is a proxy (deprecated_class, deprecated_instance) It is reported under the first public name in alphabetical order. A new alias that sorts earlier would rename it. A subpackage is scanned instead of its package with --no-recursive A re-export can be reported under another module.

The rule slugs are invalid-args, misconfigured-target, inner-order-property, identity-mapping, no-effect, positional-only-mapping, chain, expired, min-grace and message-required.

The layout is described by the JSON Schema docs/schemas/report-1.schema.json. schema is bumped only when a key is removed or renamed, or its meaning or type changes. Adding a key does not bump it, so readers must ignore keys they do not know.

The keys added in v0.16 (per-finding records, gate, mode, …) did not bump it. Every key a v0.15 report has (schema, table, gaps[].kind/detail/hint) keeps its type and meaning. A v0.15 reader therefore still reads a v0.16 report.

Report publication. The file is written only when the run exits 0 or 1. A usage error (exit 2) or crash (exit 3) leaves any existing report unchanged. Consumers must check the exit code before reading or publishing a report.

The GitHub Action builds its gap annotations and job summary from this file.

docs.title: SARIF for code scanning
docs.text:
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is the OASIS standard JSON format in which static-analysis tools report findings. Each finding includes a rule, a level, a message, a file and line, and an identifying fingerprint.

GitHub code scanning reads it to list each finding as an alert. It uses the fingerprint to recognise a finding it has already seen, avoiding duplicate alerts when code moves. See GitHub's SARIF support.

For pyDeprecate this turns an expired, min-grace or chain finding into an alert on the wrapper's decorator line, with no custom CI glue. The same file opens in any other SARIF viewer. When all you need is a pass or fail gate, skip it: the exit code and --report-json cover that.

For code scanning, --report-sarif FILE (since v0.16; every subcommand but status) writes the same run as one SARIF 2.1.0 run. The file is written only on exit 0 or 1.

SARIF content Detail Results There is one result per active finding with its level in the run, its message and its stable id. The id is the pydeprecateFindingId/v1 partial fingerprint. Rules There is one rule per check rule the subcommand evaluates. Locations A result uses a path relative to the repository root under the %SRCROOT% base. It uses the line of the wrapper's first decorator, or line 1 for a deprecated module. Files outside the root They use an absolute file: URI and are counted in a stderr advisory. Code scanning cannot match them to a repository file. Findings without a source file A finding such as a deprecated_instance data object is kept without a location and counted in run.properties.unlocated. GitHub code scanning does not display it. A run whose results all lack a location says so on stderr. Suppressed findings They are left out and counted in run.properties.suppressed. Gaps They are tool-execution notifications. run.properties.mode This is the report's mode: static for a --static run, else import.

The repository root is resolved in this order:

  1. Use the nearest directory at or above the working directory that holds .git.
  2. Otherwise use GITHUB_WORKSPACE when the working directory lies inside it.
  3. Otherwise use the working directory.

The CLI can therefore run from any directory of the checkout. Scan the package in the checkout rather than an installed copy.

PEP 702-only symbols. There is intentionally no --include-pep702 flag. Every subcommand evaluates pyDeprecate schedule metadata (deprecated_in, remove_in, a replacement) that symbols deprecated only with warnings.deprecated lack. List those with the Python API: find_deprecation_wrappers(..., include_pep702=True); see PEP 702-only deprecations.

docs.title: Policy rule flags
docs.text:
These two flags are specific to policy, one per rule. Switch them off with --min-grace=None and --message-required=False.

The Default column is the built-in value. A [tool.pydeprecate.policy] table in pyproject.toml replaces it, and a typed flag beats both.

Flag Default Rule slug Effect --min-grace=<delta> 0.3 min-grace Minimum distance between deprecated_in and remove_in as a version-shaped delta: 1.0 one major, 0.3 three minors, 0.0.2 two patches. --message-required=<bool> True message-required Require every wrapper to name a replacement (a target, a mapping, or a message_template).

The delta has two or three components with at most one non-zero. A bare 1 is rejected as ambiguous (one what?), as is a mixed spelling such as 1.2.

The removal must be one clean bump of a single component: 1.2 → 1.5 or 2.0, never 2.3. A coarser bump always clears a finer window: 0.3 is satisfied by one major bump.

Delta or project Interpretation An all-zero spelling such as 0.0 This is a zero-count window with no minimum distance. A clean bump of that unit or coarser is still required. Ten or more steps No quoting is needed on the command line: --min-grace=0.10 is ten minors. --min-grace=1.0, or min-grace = "1.0" in pyproject.toml This is the strict "removals only at a major release" policy. A 0.x project No special setting is needed. A bump to 1.0 is a major step and clears any window. Removals inside the 0.x line are counted in minors as usual.

Malformed grace windows. A malformed --min-grace value is rejected before the scan starts. It exits 2 with a message naming the accepted spellings; it is never silently ignored.

docs.title: Project configuration in pyproject.toml
docs.text:
Declare the settings once, next to the code they govern. Every bare pydeprecate run, in a developer's shell or a CI step, applies them without repeating flags:

[tool.pydeprecate]
exclude = ["my_package.tests", "*._legacy*"]   # every subcommand: the scan skips these packages (never imports them itself)
strict = true                                  # every gate subcommand: a gap fails the run (`--no-strict` overrides)
ignore = ["my_package.legacy:old_api"]         # every gate subcommand: findings accepted without a fix
baseline = "ci/pydeprecate-baseline.json"      # every gate subcommand: findings of an earlier report, by id
gate = ["policy"]                              # `all` only (since v0.16): also fail on policy violations

[tool.pydeprecate.policy]                      # the `policy` subcommand's rules, keyed by rule slug
min-grace = "0.3"  # quoted dotted delta; false switches the rule off (TOML has no null)
message-required = true

Each setting resolves independently as flag → pyproject.toml → built-in default. The Exclude: header line (printed when the list is non-empty) and the Policy: header line name the source of each value: flag, pyproject.toml, or built-in. The other settings (strict, gate, ignore, baseline) print no source line:

Exclude: my_package.tests, *._legacy* (pyproject.toml)
Policy: min-grace=0.3 (pyproject.toml)  message-required=True (built-in)

docs.title: Configuration lookup
docs.text:
The table is looked up like --version auto-detection below. Search from the scanned path's directory up to two parents. The nearest file declaring [tool.pydeprecate] wins.

There is one table per project: a nested file declaring it replaces the parent's whole table. A bare module name never triggers the lookup.

Setting Accepted values and effect exclude Patterns are fnmatch globs over the full dotted module name (my_package.tests, not tests). A pattern matching a package excludes its whole subtree. A string or comma-separated string is accepted in place of the list. min-grace It takes the dotted delta as a string ("1.0", "0.3", "0.0.2"), or a one-key unit table ({ minor = 3 }). Quote the delta ("0.10", not 0.10): a TOML float drops the trailing zero exactly as the shell does.

A wrapper is reported if and only if the module it is reported under does not match exclude. Even when something else in the package imports an excluded module, its wrappers stay out.

Configuration validation

A malformed value from the file exits 2. The message names the pyproject.toml it came from.

The following are rejected the same way:

  • message-required or strict is not a boolean.
  • An exclude or ignore entry is not a string.
  • An ignore entry is malformed.
  • A baseline file cannot be read or is not a report with a findings list.

Unknown keys in either table are reported on stderr and ignored, never silently enforced. min_grace with an underscore is the usual typo.

TOML parser required

Reading the file needs a TOML parser. It is built in on Python 3.11+; on 3.9–3.10, use the tomli backport from the [audit] extra.

Without a parser, a reachable pyproject.toml triggers a stderr advisory instead of being silently skipped. None of its [tool.pydeprecate] settings apply, including strict = true, so a gap no longer fails the run.

On Python 3.9 or 3.10, install the [audit] extra to read strict from pyproject.toml. Otherwise pass --strict on the command line.

pydeprecate all applies the same resolved settings to its single scan and its advisory policy pass.

Python policy API. The Python API (validate_deprecation_policy()) takes a module object or importable name, never a filesystem path. It does not read pyproject.toml; pass its keyword arguments, including exclude, explicitly.

docs.title: Version auto-detection
docs.text:
Every subcommand and the JSON report table use the same --version auto-detection resolver:

  1. For an existing path, search its directory and up to 2 parent directories for a pyproject.toml. The nearest file with a [project] table owns the version, even if its version cannot be resolved. Files without that table are skipped.
  2. If the local version is unresolved or the argument is a bare module name, try installed metadata in the order below.
  3. Only after these lookups fail, read the top-level import package's string __version__.

Installed metadata is tried under these names in order:

  1. Try the full import name first.
  2. Try the top-level import name next.
  3. Try the distribution that ships that top-level package, such as PIL → Pillow.

The full name takes priority because a dotted component can have a separately versioned distribution.

Lookup boundaries. An unresolved version does not fall through to an ancestor project. A bare module name skips the pyproject.toml lookup, so it cannot pick up an unrelated project's version from your current working directory.

The Python API (validate_deprecation_expiry(), generate_deprecation_table()) resolves the module's top-level package through this chain without the pyproject.toml step. It receives a module, never a path.

Only a genuinely unresolved version skips the expiry check with a version not resolved gap and exit 0, or exit 1 under --strict. Pass --version to supply it explicitly.

docs.title: Accepting known findings
docs.text:
Fix a finding when you can. When one must stay for now, accept it instead of excluding its whole module. For example, a removal might be waiting on a downstream release:

pydeprecate expiry src/mypackage --ignore='expired:mypackage.legacy:old_api'
pydeprecate all src/mypackage --report-json=ci/pydeprecate-baseline.json   # record today's backlog once
pydeprecate all src/mypackage --baseline=ci/pydeprecate-baseline.json      # later runs fail only on new findings

docs.title: Ignore patterns
docs.text:
Entry Scope module:symbol It accepts every rule of that symbol. rule:module:symbol It accepts one rule; use * for any rule. *:mypackage.compat.*:* Each part is an fnmatch glob, so this accepts everything under mypackage.compat. expired:mypackage.oldmod: The empty symbol names a deprecated module.

Commas always separate entries. A character class holding a comma such as [a,o] is therefore never one glob; write the class without commas ([ao]). The rule slugs are those of the report (expired, min-grace, chain, …).

docs.title: Baselines and suppression
docs.text:
A baseline is any --report-json file with a findings list, written since pyDeprecate v0.16. Its finding ids are accepted exactly. Ids hold no line or version, so moved code and version bumps stay accepted, and a renamed symbol is a new finding.

Ids under the file's suppressed key count only when the baseline itself suppressed them (suppressed_by.kind is baseline). A baseline regenerated from a run that used it therefore keeps them.

A finding an ignore entry suppressed is not carried over: delete the ignore entry and it is active again. There is no update flag; regenerate the file with --report-json.

Suppression detail Behaviour Both an ignore entry and the baseline name a finding It counts as ignored. Console and exit code Suppressed findings disappear from the console sections, the counts and the exit code. The run prints N finding(s) suppressed (ignore: a, baseline: b). Report It lists suppressed findings under suppressed with what matched them. Gaps and other outputs Suppressed findings never affect gaps, and SARIF and the GitHub Action never show them.

An unmatched baseline entry is reported once on stderr when all these conditions hold:

  • It matches no finding of a check that ran on its wrapper.
  • No gap such as remove_in not PEP 440 or not statically resolvable names the wrapper.
  • Its module was audited: it was inside a scanned package, not excluded, and imported without error.

The diagnostic is … baseline entries match no finding of this run (stale, or outside a narrowed scan); regenerate the baseline from a full-scope run.

The entry is counted as summary.baseline_unmatched; it never fails the run. One baseline may therefore be shared by several packages scanned in separate runs. Unused ignore entries are only counted (summary.ignore_unmatched).

docs.title: Static mode
docs.text:
pydeprecate expiry --static and pydeprecate policy --static read the package's source with Python's ast module instead of importing it. Nothing from the scanned package is imported or executed, including for the version and the --report-json table.

Use it where the package's runtime dependencies are not installed, such as the isolated environment of a remote pre-commit hook:

# phmdoctest:skip — CI template: replace src/mypackage with your package directory
pydeprecate expiry --static src/mypackage --version 2.0
pydeprecate policy --static src/mypackage

The output carries a Mode: static (source read with ast; nothing imported) header line. Recognized wrappers with resolvable settings are checked, subject to the blind spots below. A clean run does not establish complete coverage.

The source has to spell the settings a rule reads:

Rule Reads expired remove_in min-grace deprecated_in, remove_in message-required target, args_mapping, attrs_mapping, message_template

docs.title: Readable settings and forms
docs.text:
Setting form Example A literal can be read. Use remove_in="2.0". A module-level name bound once to a literal can be read. Use VERSION = "2.0". An entry of a module-level dict literal splatted into the call can be read. Use **_DEPRECATION_ARGS, bound once. Target form Interpretation A function, class or lambda, or a bare name imported from outside the scanned package It is read as a replacement. None, True, False and TargetMode members They are read as such, also through a module-level name bound once to one. That name can be bound in the same module or imported from another module of the scanned package. A deprecated_instance target that builds plain data It is read as data. As at runtime, message-required therefore needs an attrs_mapping or a message_template for it. Plain data includes a literal, a list, dict or set display, a module-level name bound once to one, or a call of a class. A call of a class the same file defines with __call__ or with bases It is a gap.

Static mode recognizes these forms:

Form Where or how it is recognized @deprecated(...) and @deprecated_callable(...) They are recognized on functions and class members. @deprecated_class(...) and @deprecated(...) They are recognized on classes. name = deprecated(...)(obj) A wrapper call is recognized. name = deprecated_class(...)(obj) A class wrapper call is recognized. name = deprecated_instance(obj, ...) An instance wrapper call is recognized. A decorator configured once and applied many times legacy = deprecated(...), then @legacy, is recognized, also when imported from another module of the package. Aliases public = _old is recognized. Inherited members Members inherited from a base class in the scanned package are recognized. deprecated_module(...) It is recognized when called in the module it deprecates. A module-level with block Code inside it is recognized.

Factory names are followed however they are imported. Examples include import deprecate as d, from deprecate.proxy import deprecated_class, from deprecate import *, or a project module that re-exports them. Rows are named and attributed as an import-mode scan does.

docs.title: Unsettled settings
docs.text:
Recognized but unresolved deprecations are reported. A form the scan recognizes as a deprecation but cannot settle from the source is reported rather than skipped. Each unsettled wrapper or setting produces one stderr line: pydeprecate gap: not statically resolvable: <file>:<line>: <reason>.

Unsettled form Detail Computed values A version computed at runtime, an f-string, or a name bound twice cannot be settled. Mutable dicts A dict changed after construction cannot be settled. Neither can a dict read other than by a ** splat or a factory keyword: an alias or helper call may change it. Rebound names Names the module rebinds through globals(), vars() or setattr(sys.modules[...], ...) cannot be settled. Expression splats Settings splatted from an expression cannot be settled. Factory placement or binding A factory used inside a function, inside if or try, or under a name also bound to something else cannot be settled. Outer decorators A decorator stacked over the factory that may replace the wrapper cannot be settled. The exceptions are property, classmethod, staticmethod, functools.lru_cache, functools.cache, abc.abstractmethod, dataclasses.dataclass and the typing markers. Attribute targets An attribute target other than a recognized TargetMode member cannot be settled. Star-import targets A target a star import may bind cannot be settled. Targets from within the package A target imported from another package module cannot be settled unless that module binds it once to a literal or a definition. Unread bases Members inherited from a base class the scan does not read cannot be settled. Star-import exports A star import cannot be settled if its __all__ is computed or the module also changes it in place or reads it (__all__.append(...)). Replaced class members A deprecated class member that an if, try or loop in the class body may replace cannot be settled. Import cycles An import cycle cannot be settled.

A module whose source cannot be parsed, or is nested too deeply to analyze, is a module not audited gap. The rest of the package is still read.

The wrapper is left out only of rules that read the unsettled setting. A version held in a variable therefore still lets message-required judge its replacement.

A module kept out of the walk by --no-recursive or --exclude is read on demand when a walked module re-exports from it. Its gap lines are printed too.

Use strict mode

A gap does not change the exit code unless strict mode is on, as with every other gap. A static run therefore passes when everything it could read is clean.

Read the gap lines, or the gaps of --report-json, to see what was not audited. Spell those settings literally to bring them into the audit.

With --strict or strict = true, a static run that recorded any gap exits 1. A CI gate that must not pass on a partly read source should enable it.

docs.title: Static version resolution
docs.text:
Without --version, the resolver tries these sources in order:

  1. Read the static [project].version of pyproject.toml.
  2. For a dynamic version, read the source the package build uses: [tool.setuptools.dynamic].version.attr, else the package's __version__.
  3. Try installed metadata.
  4. Read the __version__ literal in the package's __init__.py. Follow from .module import __version__, ... import version as __version__ and from module import * re-exports.

Rebound versions can fall back to stale metadata. A __version__ rebound inside if or try, or through a function's global, makes the source read yield nothing. It does not yield the literal before the rebinding. Resolution therefore falls back to the package's installed metadata, which may be stale for a development checkout. Pass --version explicitly in that case.

docs.title: Locations and blind spots
docs.text:
A static run's findings carry the same location as an import run's: the file and the line of the wrapper's first decorator. Results from --report-sarif therefore show in GitHub code scanning. A wrapper of an object defined in another module or bound more than once has location: null.

No gap line does not prove full coverage. Gap lines cover only what the scan recognizes, so they do not prove that nothing was missed. The blind spots below are invisible to the scan and print no gap line. A clean static run does not show they hold no deprecation.

Blind spot Detail Dynamically created wrappers Static mode cannot see wrappers created in loops or through getattr, importlib or exec. Private proxy construction It cannot see a proxy built from the private _DeprecatedProxy directly. Imported deprecated objects or configured decorators It cannot see these when imported from outside the scanned package. An import scan lists such an object under the module that re-exports it. Bare external target names from compat import NO_REPLACEMENT is read as a replacement even when it holds None or a TargetMode member, so message-required passes it. Calls to external target names A deprecated_instance target calling an external name (target=Settings()) is read as an instance of a class. message-required therefore flags it even when the call returns a callable. External factories A factory imported from outside the scanned package (from compat import deprecated, or a star import of one) is invisible. The exception is a call passing remove_in by keyword, which produces a not statically resolvable gap. Report target names Static mode cannot reproduce these exactly as import mode prints them: New API shows the source text. A dataclass whose attrs_mapping import mode expands into args_mapping reads dataclass rather than dataclass attributes.

See Limitations. Run without --static in an environment with the package's dependencies for a full audit.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Subcommand Exit 0 Exit 1 Exit 2 Exit 3 check Clean or warnings only (chains / identity / no-effect / positional-only) Invalid argument mappings, misconfigured targets or inner-order properties found A usage error (below) Scan or internal error expiry No expired wrappers; or packaging not installed or the version unresolved (gap printed; exit 1 under strict mode) Expired wrappers found Malformed --version when packaging is available; a usage error Scan or internal error policy No violations; or only a skipped min-grace rule Policy violations found Malformed rule value (flag or pyproject.toml); a usage error Scan or internal error chains No chains Deprecated-to-deprecated chains found A usage error Scan or internal error all All checks clean, or only warnings and ungated policy violations (table always appended) Any error of check, expiry or chains, and of policy with --gate=policy Malformed --version, rule value or --gate; a usage error Scan or internal error status Table rendered — status is not a pass/fail gate — Malformed --version or --style; a usage error Scan or internal error

--exit-zero turns exit 1 into 0 and never masks 2 or 3. A strict = true from pyproject.toml is switched off by a typed --exit-zero for that run; stderr says so once.

--strict (since v0.16), or strict = true in [tool.pydeprecate], adds one exit-1 reason to every subcommand but status: any recorded gap. A gap is a part of the audit that did not run, printed as a pydeprecate gap: <kind>: line. Without strict mode, gaps never change the exit code.

A strict run that fails on its gaps says so on stderr after them: Strict mode: N gap(s) fail this run.

docs.title: Usage errors
docs.text:
A usage error (exit 2) on any path stops the run before anything is scanned, on every subcommand. The following are usage errors:

Error Detail or diagnostic Malformed exclusions --exclude is malformed, whether supplied as a flag or in pyproject.toml. Unknown options An option is unknown. Invalid booleans A boolean flag has a value other than true/false/1/0. Duplicate version inputs The version is given both as the legacy second positional argument and as --version. Invalid gates --gate or gate names an unknown check or is not a list. Conflicting import names Two paths import as the same name from different places. Covered paths with independent configuration Another path's recursive scan already covers a path with its own [tool.pydeprecate] settings or, with auto-detection, its own version. Empty report paths --report-json= is empty. Conflicting exit flags --strict is typed together with --exit-zero. Invalid strict configuration A strict value in pyproject.toml is not a boolean. Invalid ignore inputs An --ignore entry is malformed, or --ignore receives a list literal. Invalid baselines A --baseline file is missing, unreadable, malformed or has no findings list, as in a report written before v0.16. Malformed means a findings or suppressed value is not a list, or an entry lacks a string id. Single files A single .py file produces File paths are not supported. Several top-level packages A directory holding two or more top-level packages produces contains multiple packages (…); pass the package sub-directory instead. Missing paths or modules A name is neither an existing path nor an importable module. This produces No such path or importable module, also for relative spellings such as ./typo or .pkg.

Missing submodules are checked during the scan. Only a missing submodule of an importable package (pkg.nosuch) is found when its own path is scanned. With several paths, the ones before it are scanned first. It still exits 2 with no report.

With --static, these are also usage errors:

Error Detail or diagnostic Unsupported subcommand The flag is used on a subcommand other than expiry and policy: --static, --no-static and --nostatic are supported by `expiry` and `policy` only, not `check`. Dotted module names Locating one would import its parent packages; pass its directory instead. Modules without Python source A built-in or compiled module has no Python source.

docs.title: Scan and internal errors
docs.text:
Exit 3 means the audit itself did not run. Neither error writes a --report-json file.

Diagnostic Meaning pydeprecate: scan error: … The scanned package cannot be imported because its module-level code raises or exits. This never occurs with --static, which imports nothing. pydeprecate: internal error: … There is a bug in the CLI. The diagnostic includes the issue tracker to report it to.

Submodule failures. A submodule that fails is a module not audited gap unless explicitly requested. When explicitly requested, the run exits 3 even when a parent scan covers it.

Policy violations are the one finding all reports without acting on by default: they move all from 0 to 1 only with --gate=policy.

Unknown or misspelled flags are never silently ignored. For example, pydeprecate expiry mypackage --verison 2.0 exits 2 with an unrecognized arguments: --verison diagnostic before anything is scanned.

docs.title: CI recipes
docs.text:
Use pydeprecate all --gate=policy (since v0.16) for one step and one scan. It fails the build on misconfigured wrappers, chains, expired deprecations, and deprecations scheduled in a way the project does not allow. The console sections and the report's rule field tell you which problem you have.

A monorepo passes every package to the same step. The full workflow, with the rules declared once in [tool.pydeprecate.policy], is in the audit guide.

While bringing an existing codebase into line, follow these steps:

  1. Run the gate advisory-first so it reports without blocking.
  2. Drop the flag once the backlog is clear.
pydeprecate policy src/mypackage --exit-zero

On GitHub Actions the CLI also ships as a ready-made step, uses: Borda/pyDeprecate@<tag>; the step exits with the CLI's own code. See the GitHub Action section of the audit guide for every input and output.

docs.title: Path formats
docs.text:
All subcommands accept these path formats:

Format Behaviour Package directory Provide a path to a directory with __init__.py, such as src/mypackage. Importable module name Provide a dotted module path such as mypackage.utils in import mode. Static mode accepts only top-level module names. Plain directory The scan reads top-level .py files only. Nested files are reported as a nested files not audited gap. No path The scan picks the single package under src/, else the single package at the repository root. With several packages the run fails, so pass the path.

The subcommand may be omitted too: pydeprecate src/mypackage runs check.

Unsupported paths. A single .py file, or a directory holding two or more top-level packages, is a usage error (exit 2) for every subcommand.

While scanning, the imported code sees no pydeprecate arguments in sys.argv. The header line Imported from: names the file the package was actually imported from.

docs.title: Python module invocation
docs.text:
Both pydeprecate and python -m deprecate are equivalent entry points:

python -m deprecate check src/mypackage
python -m deprecate expiry src/mypackage --version 2.0.0

Module invocation is useful where the pydeprecate script is not on PATH, such as a Docker image where only python is available.

docs.title: Enforcing Removal Deadlines
docs.text:
remove_in commits you to delete code when that version ships. Forgotten deadlines leave zombie code behind.

validate_deprecation_expiry() scans a module or package for every deprecated callable whose removal version has been reached or passed. It returns error-message strings. An empty list means the scan found no expired callables.

Install the audit extra for packaging, which provides PEP 440 version comparison:

pip install 'pyDeprecate[audit]'

Scan a package and control recursion depth:

from deprecate import validate_deprecation_expiry

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package

# Scan your package for expired deprecations - using early-version that won't have expirations
expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package, "0.2")
print(f"Found {len(expired)} expired")  # Returns a list of error messages (empty list = no expired)

# Example with expired deprecations found (using later-version)
expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package, "0.5")
print(f"Found {len(expired)} expired")

# Auto-detect version from package metadata (mocked for demo)
from unittest.mock import patch

with patch("importlib.metadata.version", return_value="0.3"):
    expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package)  # Automatically detects version
    print(f"Found {len(expired)} expired")

# Control recursion
expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package, "0.1", recursive=False)  # Only scan top-level module
print(f"Found {len(expired)} expired")
Output: f"Found {len(expired)} expired" 
Found 14 expired
Found 31 expired
Found 17 expired
Found 0 expired

Expiry scope and comparison follow these rules:

Setting or input Behavior include_members=True (default) Include class members decorated with @deprecated, such as an __init__ wrapped by deprecated_class delegation. include_members=False Restrict discovery to module-level callables. No remove_in Skip the callable; notice-only deprecations are allowed. PEP 440 versions Compare versions normally, such as "2.0.0" > "1.9.5". Pre-release versions Order them correctly, such as "1.5.0a1" < "1.5.0".

Unparsable versions leave gaps

An invalid remove_in is skipped with a UserWarning naming the callable and unparsable version. Its expiry is not checked. The CLI prints a remove_in not PEP 440 gap instead.

pydeprecate policy also prints gaps for versions its min-grace rule cannot parse. These are remove_in not PEP 440 or deprecated_in not PEP 440 gaps. A --strict run fails on them.

A downstream release may still need a symbol past its deadline. Accept that finding without excluding the whole module using the CLI ignore list or a baseline report. See Accepting known findings. The Python API returns every finding and has no ignore or baseline filter, so your code decides which findings to keep.

docs.title: pytest integration for expiry enforcement
docs.text:
Wire expiry checks into your test suite so zombie code is caught before any tests run. The session-scoped autouse fixture pattern below prevents the suite from starting at all if expired deprecations are present.

import pytest
from deprecate import validate_deprecation_expiry

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package


def test_no_zombie_deprecations():
    """Ensure all deprecated code is removed when it reaches its deadline."""
    # Use your package's actual version - for this example we use a test version
    current_version = "0.5"  # Replace with: from mypackage import __version__

    expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package, current_version)

    if expired:
        error_msg = "Found deprecated code past its removal deadline:\n"
        for msg in expired:
            error_msg += f"  - {msg}\n"
        pytest.fail(error_msg)


# Alternative: Use a fixture to run on every test session
# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
@pytest.fixture(scope="session", autouse=True)
def enforce_deprecation_deadlines():
    """Automatically check for zombie code before running any tests."""
    from tests.collections.api_deprecated import core as my_package

    current_version = "0.5"  # Replace with: from mypackage import __version__
    expired = validate_deprecation_expiry(my_package, current_version)
    if expired:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"Cannot run tests: {len(expired)} deprecated callables past removal deadline. "
            f"Remove these functions first: {expired}"
        )

docs.title: Enforcing a Deprecation Policy
docs.text:
validate_deprecation_expiry() asks whether code was removed on time. validate_deprecation_policy() checks whether the original schedule and migration guidance were responsible.

It detects short upgrade windows, removals off release boundaries, and warnings that name no replacement. These problems are cheap to fix during review. They become expensive once downstream projects pin against the release.

Like the expiry gate, the policy gate compares PEP 440 versions and therefore needs the audit extra:

pip install 'pyDeprecate[audit]'

Set up a policy in two steps:

  1. Declare the rules once in pyproject.toml:

    [tool.pydeprecate.policy]
min-grace = "1.0"
message-required = true

  2. Run the gate locally or in CI. See Enforcing the policy in CI:

    pydeprecate policy src/mypackage

min-grace is a version-shaped delta:

Value Required window "1.0" Removal is allowed only at the next major. "0.3" (built-in default) Callers receive three minors. "0.0.2" Callers receive two patches. false The rule is disabled.

Each run resolves each rule in this order: flag, project table, built-in default. A Policy: header identifies the source. See project configuration.

The Python function takes rules as arguments. It never reads the configuration file.

docs.title: The two rules
docs.text:
Rule slug What it checks Default Disable with min-grace remove_in is one clean version bump beyond deprecated_in, at least this far min_grace="0.3" min_grace=None message-required The wrapper provides migration guidance (a target, a mapping, or a custom message) message_required=True message_required=False

Every violation message starts with its rule slug in square brackets: [min-grace] or [message-required]. Group or filter CI logs by that stable prefix without parsing the prose.

Tune the defaults using these contracts.

docs.title: Grace windows
docs.text:
min_grace accepts a version-shaped delta string with two or three components. At most one component may be non-zero.

Input Interpretation "1.0" One major. "0.3" Three minors. "0.0.2" Two patches. "1" Reject as ambiguous: the unit is unknown. "1.2", or another mixed spelling Reject before scanning with ValueError. "0.0" Accept a zero-count minor window.

Pass version deltas as strings

A float such as 0.10 loses its trailing zero and reads as one minor. Always pass the version-shaped form as a string.

Zero-count windows still require clean bumps. An all-zero window effectively disables the distance check. A clean bump of that unit or coarser remains required. Thus, 1.2 → 1.2.1 violates a zero-minor window.

Internally, every spelling becomes deprecate.audit.GraceWindow(count, unit): one unit and one count. The scan consults only this parsed window.

You may also pass a GraceWindow instance (from deprecate import GraceWindow, VersionBump) or a one-key unit table such as {"major": 1}.

The removal must cleanly bump a single component and reset every lower component. For example, 1.2 → 1.5 or 2.0 is valid. 1.2 → 2.3 or 1.3.1 is not.

Mixed bumps miss the release boundaries on which projects promise removals.

Relative unit Result A coarser bump than the window. It always clears the window. Deprecation in 1.2 and removal in 2.0 satisfies "0.3", despite the lower minor number. A finer bump than the window. It never clears the window. A patch cannot satisfy a minor-counted window.

Projects before 1.0

A 0.x project needs no special setting. A bump to 1.0 is a major step and clears any window. Removals within 0.x are counted in minors as usual.

min_grace="1.0" enforces the strict policy of removals only at a major.

docs.title: Migration guidance
docs.text:
message_required accepts these forms of guidance:

  • A callable or module target names a replacement.
  • An args_mapping names argument replacements.
  • An attrs_mapping names attribute replacements.
  • A custom message_template supplies guidance.

Guidance edge cases

An empty args_mapping or attrs_mapping ({}) carries no actual rename. The rule treats it like no mapping.

A deprecated module passes with a custom message_template. The auto-rendered text stored by deprecated_module() does not count; otherwise, every module would pass trivially. A module using only target or attrs_mapping needs at least one non-empty value.

A deprecated_instance() proxy over a dict or settings instance needs a custom message_template or an attrs_mapping for the default policy. The object is never called, so its args_mapping never applies. A target= replacement is served under the old name but is absent from the built-in warning.

docs.title: Scanning a package
docs.text:
from deprecate import validate_deprecation_policy

# For testing purposes, we use the test module; normally you would import your own package
from tests.collections import policy as my_package

# Full default policy: a three-minor grace window on a clean release boundary, guidance required
violations = validate_deprecation_policy(my_package, recursive=False)
print(f"Found {len(violations)} violations")

# Every message is prefixed with the slug of the rule it broke
for msg in sorted(violations):
    print(msg.split("]")[0] + "]")

# Opt out of the grace-window rule, keep the guidance rule
violations = validate_deprecation_policy(my_package, recursive=False, min_grace=None)
print(f"Found {len(violations)} violations")
Output: f"Found {len(violations)} violations" 
Found 7 violations
[message-required]
[message-required]
[message-required]
[message-required]
[min-grace]
[min-grace]
[min-grace]
Found 4 violations

Wrappers without deprecated_in or remove_in do not violate the grace-window rule. That rule skips them because unscheduled deprecations are valid and common.

An unparsable version emits a UserWarning naming the wrapper and offending field. The scan continues, so one typo never aborts the gate.

recursive, include_members, and exclude behave exactly as in find_deprecation_wrappers().

Result formats

Policy results are message strings, not structured records. Filter, group, or suppress them by the stable [min-grace] or [message-required] slug. The wording after that prefix may change.

validate_deprecation_expiry() also returns plain strings, without a slug. Use find_deprecation_wrappers() for structured per-wrapper DeprecationWrapperInfo rows.

The CLI's --report-json contains the rendered deprecation table, run gaps, and structured finding records with violation messages (since v0.16). See the CLI Reference.

The CLI exposes the same gate as pydeprecate policy. See the CLI Reference for flags and exit codes. See Enforcing the policy in CI for workflow wiring.

The CLI can read [tool.pydeprecate.policy] from pyproject.toml. See project configuration.

The Python function accepts a module object or importable name, never a filesystem path. It does not read that file. Pass min_grace and message_required explicitly.

docs.title: API documentation integration
docs.text: Enable update_docstring=True to include migration notices in API documentation. Then configure the documentation engine to read those runtime docstrings.

docs.title: Update docstrings
docs.text:
The decorator updates an existing docstring at decoration time; it does not wait for a deprecated call.

from deprecate import deprecated, void

# NEW API — adds quantities using the replacement implementation
from tests.collections.api_current.core import base_sum_kwargs


# DEPRECATED API — `calculate_total` replaced by `base_sum_kwargs`
@deprecated(
    target=base_sum_kwargs,
    deprecated_in="0.1",
    remove_in="0.5",
    update_docstring=True,
    docstring_style="rst",
)
def calculate_total(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    """Add invoice line quantities."""
    return void(a, b)


print(calculate_total.__doc__)
Output: calculate_total.__doc__ 
Add invoice line quantities.

.. deprecated:: 0.1
   Will be removed in 0.5.
   Use :func:`tests.collections.api_current.core.base_sum_kwargs` instead.

The option is named update_docstring and defaults to False on deprecated, deprecated_callable and deprecated_class; deprecated_instance and deprecated_module have no such option, so they inject no docstring notice. The notice includes the removal version when supplied, and a replacement reference when target is callable.

docstring_style Injected format "rst" A Sphinx .. deprecated:: directive. "mkdocs" A Markdown !!! warning "Deprecated in …" admonition. "markdown" An alias for "mkdocs". "auto" (default) Select the format from the build environment.

Automatic selection checks these signals in order:

  1. A recognized DEPRECATE_DOCSTRING_STYLE value: rst, mkdocs, or markdown.
  2. The presence of mkdocs in sys.modules.
  3. The text mkdocs in the executable path, sys.argv[0].
  4. The fallback format, "rst".

Choose explicitly when needed

An explicit docstring_style bypasses automatic detection. Unsupported values raise ValueError at decoration time, even with update_docstring=False.

docs.title: Sphinx
docs.text:
Add deprecate.docstring.sphinx_ext to extensions in conf.py alongside autodoc.

# phmdoctest:skip — Sphinx conf.py configuration snippet
extensions = [
    "sphinx.ext.autodoc",
    "sphinx.ext.napoleon",  # Parse Google-style or NumPy-style docstrings.
    "deprecate.docstring.sphinx_ext",
]

autoclass_content = "both"
autodoc_default_options = {
    "members": True,
    "undoc-members": True,
    "show-inheritance": True,
}
  • Use docstring_style="rst" on wrappers intended for Sphinx.
  • Document functions with autofunction and classes with autoclass.
  • Install Sphinx and make pyDeprecate and the documented package importable in the build environment.

Autodoc reads function docstrings at runtime. The bundled extension handles the proxies returned by deprecated_class, which otherwise appear as aliases without their injected notices.

It uses the wrapped class for signature and member inspection, while retaining the proxy's updated docstring. The rendered class entry therefore includes the deprecation notice instead of only an “alias of” description.

Configuration scope

The extension defines no additional Sphinx configuration keys. autoclass_content and autodoc_default_options are autodoc settings. Both bundled documentation extensions are beta; their public interfaces may change in a minor release.

See the repository's Sphinx configuration and API directives for a complete example.

docs.title: MkDocs and mkdocstrings
docs.text:
Configure deprecate.docstring.griffe_ext:RuntimeDocstrings under the Python handler's options.extensions.

markdown_extensions:
  - admonition

plugins:
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          paths: ["src"]
          options:
            docstring_style: google
            extensions:
              - deprecate.docstring.griffe_ext:RuntimeDocstrings

Use update_docstring=True and docstring_style="mkdocs" on decorated APIs to produce Markdown notices. This repository uses the same Griffe extension in its own mkdocs.yml.

Two different style options

The decorator's docstring_style="mkdocs" selects the injected notice format. The handler's docstring_style: google selects how mkdocstrings parses the surrounding docstring.

Griffe normally reads docstrings from the source syntax tree, which does not contain decoration-time changes. RuntimeDocstrings imports the documented module and replaces matching function, class, and method docstrings with their runtime values.

  1. Install mkdocstrings[python] and pyDeprecate in the documentation environment.
  2. Set paths to the documented source location and make its runtime dependencies available.
  3. Add the extension and enable admonition as shown above.
  4. Render the API with a mkdocstrings directive such as deprecate.deprecated.

Runtime imports

The Griffe extension executes module imports during the build. It leaves docstrings unchanged when its import attempts fail with ImportError. Other import-time exceptions can fail the build.

See the repository's MkDocs demo for a complete configuration.

docs.title: Placement and limits
docs.text:
• Without args_mapping, general notices precede the first recognized Google-style or NumPy-style section, or follow the docstring when no section exists.
  • With args_mapping, Google-style Args: / Arguments: and Sphinx :param entries receive inline notes for deprecated arguments.
  • With TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, finding every deprecated argument suppresses the general notice because only arguments are deprecated.
  • MkDocs shows the notice only for the decorator form: Griffe reads a call-form alias such as Old = deprecated_class(...)(New) as an attribute with no docstring, so it gets no notice.
  • Callable targets still receive a general notice after inline argument annotations. Missing argument entries also cause a general notice.

Existing text is required: update_docstring=True leaves a missing or empty docstring unchanged. The Griffe extension also requires an existing static docstring and deprecation metadata. It does not create documentation for undocumented objects.

See Functions for argument migrations, Classes for proxy behavior, and Advanced for more docstring examples.

docs.title: Testing Deprecated Code
docs.text:
assert_no_warnings fails if a specified warning category is raised inside its context block. Pair it with pytest.warns to test both the presence and absence of deprecation notices.

num_warns defaults to 1, limiting the deprecation message to one emission per function lifetime.

The first test checks that the warning appears. The third checks the default silence on subsequent calls.

from deprecate import deprecated, assert_no_warnings, void
import pytest


# NEW API — doubles the input value
def score_predictions(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2


# DEPRECATED API — `score` replaced by `score_predictions`
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def score(x: int) -> int:
    pass


# DEPRECATED API — `score_v2` replaced by `score_predictions`
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def score_v2(x: int) -> int:
    return void(x)


def test_deprecated_function_shows_warning():
    """Verify the deprecation warning is shown."""
    with pytest.warns(FutureWarning, match="score.*deprecated"):
        result = score(42)
    assert result == 84


def test_new_function_no_warning():
    """Verify new function doesn't trigger warnings."""
    with assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning):
        result = score_predictions(42)
    assert result == 84


def test_no_warning_after_first_call():
    """By default, warnings are shown only once per function."""
    # First call shows warning
    with pytest.warns(FutureWarning):
        score_v2(1)

    # Subsequent calls don't show warning (by default num_warns=1)
    with assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning):
        score_v2(2)


# call the tests for CI demonstration/validation
test_deprecated_function_shows_warning()
test_new_function_no_warning()
test_no_warning_after_first_call()
print("Warning tests passed")
Output: "Warning tests passed" 
Warning tests passed

Use these warning budgets to test repeated calls:

Setting Behavior Use num_warns=-1 Warn on every call. Make critical deprecations impossible to miss. num_warns=N Warn exactly N times. Verify emission counts precisely in integration tests. 
# NEW API — doubles the input value
def score_predictions(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2


# ---------------------------

from deprecate import deprecated


# DEPRECATED API — `predict` replaced by `score_predictions`; warn on every call
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0", num_warns=-1)
def predict(x: int) -> int:
    pass


# DEPRECATED API — `predict_batch` replaced by `score_predictions`; warn five times
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0", num_warns=5)
def predict_batch(x: int) -> int:
    pass


print(predict_batch(1))
Output: predict_batch(1) 
2

docs.title: Suppressing warnings in test fixtures
docs.text:
A deprecated call in test setup still emits its first FutureWarning. This includes fixtures, factory helpers, and shared utilities. With default num_warns=1, subsequent calls are silent.

To exercise forwarding with clean pytest output, suppress the specific message at test-session level in pyproject.toml:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
filterwarnings = [
    'ignore:The `create_session` was deprecated:FutureWarning',
]

Alternatively, configure the equivalent runtime filter in conftest.py:

# phmdoctest:skip — pytest conftest.py configuration snippet, not a runnable example
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="The `create_session` was deprecated", category=FutureWarning)

Keep filters specific

Filter the deprecation message rather than the entire FutureWarning category. Unrelated deprecations from dependencies must remain visible.

from deprecate import deprecated, assert_no_warnings, void


# NEW API — creates a session dict with host and timeout
def new_create_session(host: str, timeout: int = 30) -> dict:
    return {"host": host, "timeout": timeout}


# DEPRECATED API — `create_session` replaced by `new_create_session`
@deprecated(target=new_create_session, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def create_session(host: str, timeout: int = 30) -> dict:
    return void(host, timeout)


def make_test_session(host: str = "localhost") -> dict:
    """Test fixture helper — calls deprecated API."""
    return create_session(host, timeout=5)  # warns: FutureWarning


# The first call emits one FutureWarning (suppressed in pytest by the filter above):
session = make_test_session()
print(session)

# Meanwhile, assert_no_warnings verifies NEW code is clean:
with assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning):
    clean_session = new_create_session("prod.example.com")
print(clean_session)
Output: new_create_session("prod.example.com") 
{'host': 'localhost', 'timeout': 5}
{'host': 'prod.example.com', 'timeout': 30}

docs.title: Choosing the right testing tool
docs.text:
Tool Use when... Behaviour pytest.warns(FutureWarning) Testing that a deprecated function DOES warn on first call Fails if no matching warning is raised assert_no_warnings() (no argument) Testing that no warning of any type is raised Fails if any warning is raised assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning) Testing that new code or subsequent calls do NOT warn Fails if a matching warning IS raised assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning, match="pattern") Testing that a specific warning message is absent Only fails if a warning matching the pattern is raised filterwarnings config (pyproject.toml / conftest.py) Calling deprecated code in fixtures/setup without assertion Silently suppresses matching warnings; never fails

Substring matching

assert_no_warnings accepts a substring through match. It checks the captured warnings' message content. You can forbid one specific deprecation while allowing unrelated warnings.

docs.title: Failing the suite on deprecated calls
docs.text: To fail a run when your own code still calls a deprecated API, make deprecations fatal for the suite: DEPRECATE_AS_EXCEPTIONS=1 pytest turns every deprecation that defers to the global switch into a DeprecatedError. To scope it to one stretch of code, wrap it in the as_exceptions() context manager, or exempt a block from a strict run with as_exceptions(False). See Fatal deprecations for the semantics.
