docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
This page covers these deprecation patterns for Python functions and methods:

  • Forward calls to a replacement.
  • Rename arguments.
  • Emit a notice with no replacement.
  • Remap arguments within the same function.
  • Stack multiple decorators.
  • Suppress deprecations conditionally.

For class deprecation see Classes; for async functions see Async.

@deprecated vs. deprecated_callable

@deprecated is the friendly front door. Applied to a function, method, or other callable/descriptor, it behaves exactly as documented on this page.

Applied to a class, it dispatches to deprecated_class with a one-time informational notice rather than raising an error.

Use deprecated_callable() for a strict, callable-only form, for example to enforce "only functions here". It shares every parameter with @deprecated and raises TypeError immediately when applied to a class at decoration time.

docs.title: Simple function forwarding
docs.text:
Body is dead code when target=<callable>

When target is a callable, pyDeprecate intercepts every call before the function body runs. The body is dead code under normal forwarding.

Exception: if you also use skip_if and it evaluates True at call time, the source body executes as a fallback. In that case keep a working body; otherwise skip_if=True calls silently return None.

Do not call the target from inside the body:

from deprecate import deprecated, void


def score_predictions(val: int) -> int:
    return val * 2


# WRONG — score_predictions(val) is never reached; the decorator forwards before the body runs
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def score(val: int) -> int:
    return score_predictions(val)


# CORRECT — body is empty; pyDeprecate handles all forwarding automatically
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def score(val: int) -> int:
    return void(val)  # or: pass  or: """Original function description."""

Apply @deprecated(target=<callable>) to the old name. pyDeprecate forwards every call, including positional and keyword arguments, to the new function.

Under normal forwarding the body is dead code, so leave it empty or put a docstring there. See also void() helper for a null-forwarding idiom.

Keep a fallback body with skip_if. The one exception is skip_if=True at call time, when the source body executes as a fallback. Keep a working body when combining target=<callable> with skip_if; see the danger admonition above.

The warning fires when the deprecated function is used:

Function kind Warning timing Regular function When the function is called. async def function When the coroutine is awaited. Generator or async generator function On the first next() / async for step; see Advanced and Async.

Defining or importing the function does not warn. Importing a module that merely defines deprecated functions therefore stays silent.

Deprecated decorators warn at definition time. A deprecated function used as a decorator is the one exception. Applying it with @ calls it at the def statement, so it warns at definition time. See this troubleshooting answer and issue #96.

# NEW/FUTURE API — renamed to be more explicit about what it computes
def compute(a: int = 0, b: int = 3) -> int:
    """New function anywhere in the codebase or even other package."""
    return a + b


# ---------------------------

from deprecate import deprecated


# What this module looked like before the rename:
# def calculate(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
#     return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — `calculate` was the original name before the rename
@deprecated(target=compute, deprecated_in="0.1", remove_in="0.5")
def calculate(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    """
    My deprecated function which now has an empty body
     as all calls are routed to the new function.
    """
    pass  # or you can just place docstring as one above


# calling this function will raise a deprecation warning:
#   The `calculate` was deprecated since v0.1 in favor of `your_module.compute`.
#   It will be removed in v0.5.
print(calculate(1, 2))
Output: calculate(1, 2) 
3

If the deprecated name already exists as a callable, apply deprecated() directly as a wrapper call instead of using decorator syntax. The callable might be imported from another package. This works on any callable, including ones you do not control.

from deprecate import deprecated


# NEW/FUTURE API — in real usage this would be imported from another module
def compute_sum(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int:
    return a + b


# LEGACY — already-existing callable that is being deprecated
def addition(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int:
    return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — `calculate` was the original name in this package;
# wrap it without redefining a function body
calculate = deprecated(
    target=compute_sum,
    deprecated_in="0.5",
    remove_in="1.0",
)(addition)
print(calculate(1, 2))
Output: calculate(1, 2) 
3

docs.title: Partial and callable-instance targets
docs.text:
target accepts any callable, including a named function, a class, a functools.partial that presets arguments, or an instance with __call__.

The warning names what a caller can import:

  • For a partial, it names the wrapped function or class, using the innermost one for a nested partial.
  • For a callable instance, it names the instance's class.

deprecated_class accepts a partial target too, for example partial(NewWidget, theme="dark"). @deprecated on a class forwards only a class target, so use deprecated_class(target=...) for a function or partial target.

A keyword the partial binds is the replacement's intended value, so the source's own default for that argument is not forwarded over it.

Per argument, values take precedence in this order:

  1. A value the caller passes, by keyword or by position, takes priority.
  2. The keyword the partial binds takes priority over the source default.
  3. The source default applies last.
from functools import partial

from deprecate import deprecated


# NEW API — general rounding helper; the precision is a parameter
def round_amount(amount: float, digits: int = 0) -> float:
    return round(amount, digits)


# DEPRECATED API — `round_price` always rounded to cents; it now forwards to `round_amount` with `digits=2` preset
@deprecated(target=partial(round_amount, digits=2), deprecated_in="0.5", remove_in="1.0")
def round_price(amount: float, digits: int = 4) -> float:
    pass


print(round_price(3.14159))  # warns: FutureWarning
print(round_price(3.14159, digits=3))
Output: round_price(3.14159), round_price(3.14159, digits=3) 
3.14
3.142

The first call gets the partial's digits=2, not the source default digits=4; the second call's explicit digits=3 wins over both. The warning names the function the partial wraps: The `round_price` was deprecated since v0.5 in favor of `your_module.round_amount`. ….

Positional arguments bound by a partial are not supported. pyDeprecate forwards arguments by name. A slot the partial binds positionally is no longer a parameter of the partial.

With partial(round_amount, 3.14159), the first call therefore raises TypeError: Failed mapping of `round_price`, arguments not accepted by target: ['amount']. Bind keywords only (partial(round_amount, digits=2)).

A functools.partial, partialmethod or singledispatchmethod cannot be the decorated source. None has a function body for the wrapper to take over, so @deprecated raises TypeError naming the type. Wrap the alias in a plain def that calls it and decorate that function instead.

docs.title: Argument renaming and mapping
docs.text:
Use args_mapping when the new function accepts the same arguments under different names. The decorator translates old parameter names to new ones at call time. Callers can keep passing the old names during the deprecation window without any manual mapping code.

import logging
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from deprecate import deprecated, void


@deprecated(
    # use standard sklearn accuracy implementation
    target=accuracy_score,
    # custom warning stream
    stream=logging.warning,
    # number of warnings per lifetime (with -1 for always)
    num_warns=5,
    # lifecycle metadata shown in notices and audit output
    deprecated_in="0.6",
    remove_in="1.0",
    # custom message template
    message_template="`%(source_name)s` was deprecated, use `%(target_path)s`",
    # as target args are different, define mapping from source to target func
    args_mapping={"preds": "y_pred", "target": "y_true", "blabla": None},
)
def depr_accuracy(preds: list, target: list, blabla: float) -> float:
    """My deprecated function which is mapping to sklearn accuracy."""
    # to stop complain your IDE about unused argument you can use void/empty function
    return void(preds, target, blabla)


# calling this function will raise a deprecation warning:
#   WARNING:root:`depr_accuracy` was deprecated, use `sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score`
print(depr_accuracy([1, 0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 1, 2], 1.23))

Passing both old and new argument names at once

If a caller supplies both the deprecated name and its replacement in one call, the explicit new-name value always wins. For example, this applies to fn(val=5, new_val=6). The remapped old-name value is silently discarded.

To make this visible, pyDeprecate also emits a UserWarning alongside the regular FutureWarning:

UserWarning: Both `val` (deprecated) and `new_val` were supplied to `fn()`; `val` is ignored.

Clean up the call site by removing the deprecated argument name.

docs.title: Notice-only deprecation
docs.text:
The function body still executes with TargetMode.NOTIFY — keep a working implementation

TargetMode.NOTIFY runs the original function body after emitting the deprecation notice. You must keep a working implementation in the function body. An empty body (pass) returns None instead of the intended value, although the deprecation warning still fires.

With target=<callable>, the body is dead code under normal forwarding. It still executes as a fallback when skip_if=True at call time.

Use warn-only mode when a function is going away but has no replacement yet. This is the right choice when callers need to update their own code, not switch to a different function.

The decorator emits a deprecation notice and then runs the function body normally. The source receives the caller's arguments unchanged. A functools.singledispatch function or a source with a custom __signature__ therefore dispatches exactly as it does undecorated.

An invalid call raises the same TypeError the undecorated function would, after the deprecation notice. Examples include a value passed both positionally and by keyword, or a positional-only parameter passed by keyword.

Prefer spelling out target=TargetMode.NOTIFY — it makes the warn-only intent explicit at the call site. If you omit target, the TargetMode.AUTO default resolves to TargetMode.NOTIFY when no args_mapping is given, so this shorter form is equivalent:

from deprecate import deprecated


@deprecated(deprecated_in="0.1", remove_in="0.5")
def my_sum(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    """My deprecated function which still has to have implementation."""
    return a + b


# calling this function will raise a deprecation warning:
#   The `my_sum` was deprecated since v0.1. It will be removed in v0.5.
print(my_sum(1, 2))
Output: my_sum(1, 2) 
3

docs.title: Rename arguments within one function
docs.text:
Use TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP to rename or drop an argument within the same function. The decorator remaps the old argument name before the body runs, so your implementation only needs the new name. This is the right pattern when refactoring a signature without moving the function.

Pass target=TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP explicitly alongside args_mapping for the recommended, self-documenting form.

On @deprecated, omitting target also works: a bare args_mapping auto-resolves via the TargetMode.AUTO default. The strict deprecated_callable() form always requires the explicit target.

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated


@deprecated(
    # rename an argument within the same function
    target=TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP,
    args_mapping={"coef": "new_coef"},
    # common version info
    deprecated_in="0.2",
    remove_in="0.4",
)
def any_pow(base: float, coef: float = 0, new_coef: float = 0) -> float:
    """My function with deprecated argument `coef` mapped to `new_coef`."""
    return base**new_coef


# calling this function will raise a deprecation warning:
#   The `any_pow` uses deprecated arguments: `coef` -> `new_coef`.
#   They were deprecated since v0.2 and will be removed in v0.4.
print(any_pow(2, 3))
Output: any_pow(2, 3) 
8

To drop an argument entirely, map it to None. The decorator emits a deprecation notice when the argument is passed and then discards it.

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated
from typing import Optional


@deprecated(
    target=TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP,
    args_mapping={"num_workers": None},
    deprecated_in="1.8",
    remove_in="1.9",
)
def my_func(value: int, num_workers: Optional[int] = None) -> int:
    """num_workers is no longer used; omit it (auto-detected)."""
    return value * 2


# Passing the removed argument triggers a warning and the argument is silently discarded:
#   The `my_func` uses deprecated arguments: `num_workers` -> `None`.
#   They were deprecated since v1.8 and will be removed in v1.9.
print(my_func(value=42, num_workers=4))
Output: my_func(value=42, num_workers=4) 
84

Only None drops an argument. A mapped value of "" (empty string) keeps the argument under its old name. It is passed through to the function unchanged, and the deprecation notice still fires.

Changed in v0.15

deprecated_class proxies have always behaved this way; @deprecated now matches them. This changed in v0.15; before it, @deprecated dropped an argument mapped to "" just like one mapped to None. If you relied on that, map the argument to None instead.

docs.title: TargetMode.NOTIFY vs TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP vs target=<callable> — key differences
docs.text:
These modes differ in whether the function body runs, whether a warning fires, and which parameters take effect.

Mode defaults

TargetMode.NOTIFY replaces the old target=None sentinel and TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP replaces the old target=True sentinel. The old forms still work but emit a FutureWarning at decoration time.

On @deprecated, target defaults to TargetMode.AUTO. This fallback resolves an omitted target at decoration time:

Mapping Resolved mode Non-empty args_mapping ARGS_REMAP No mapping, including an empty {} NOTIFY

The resolved mode, never AUTO itself, is stored in DeprecationConfig. Prefer passing the explicit mode so intent is visible at the call site.

The front door accepts target=TargetMode.AUTO written out. It is identical to omitting target and conveys nothing extra. The strict deprecated_callable(), whose default is TargetMode.NOTIFY, raises TypeError if you try.

docs.title: Behaviour comparison
docs.text:
TargetMode.NOTIFY TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP (with args_mapping) target=<callable> Warning emitted Yes — up to num_warns times (default: once) Per deprecated arg, up to num_warns times (default: once) Yes — up to num_warns times (default: once) Warning template "… was deprecated since vX. It will be removed in vY." "… uses deprecated arguments: …" "… was deprecated … in favour of …" message_template specifiers source_name, source_path, deprecated_in, remove_in only — target_name/target_path unavailable source_name, source_path, argument_map, deprecated_in, remove_in All specifiers incl. target_name, target_path Function body Runs with the caller's arguments unchanged Runs after argument renaming/dropping Does not run under normal forwarding — body is dead code, calls intercepted first. Exception: skip_if=True at call time bypasses forwarding and executes the source body as fallback args_mapping applied ⚠ ✓ renames or drops listed args ✓ renames or drops args before forwarding args_extra injected ⚠ ✓ merged into kwargs before call ✓ merged into kwargs before forwarding Source defaults merged ✗ ✗ ✓ skip_if effect ⊛ ⊛ ⊛ stream=None effect ⊘ body still runs ⊘ remapping still runs ⊘ forwarding still runs

Legend:

Symbol Meaning ✓ The option is applied. ✗ The option is not applied. ⚠ The option is ignored with UserWarning; this will be TypeError in v1.0. ⊘ The warning is suppressed, but processing continues. ⊛ skip_if bypasses everything. — The option is not applicable.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text: Mode When to use it Behaviour TargetMode.NOTIFY The function is going away with no replacement; callers must remove the call. The warning fires up to num_warns times per wrapper (default: once); the first call exhausts the default budget. target=<callable> The function is replaced by another callable. Use args_mapping to rename arguments and args_extra to inject new required args. The source body never runs under normal forwarding. The exception is skip_if=True, which bypasses forwarding and executes the source body as fallback. TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP + args_mapping The function stays but its signature is changing. The warning fires only when the old argument name is actually used. Callers who already migrated see no noise.

docs.title: Example — notice the difference in warning behaviour
docs.text:
from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated


# TargetMode.NOTIFY: warns once by default (num_warns=1)
@deprecated(target=TargetMode.NOTIFY, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def going_away(val: int) -> int:
    return val


# TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP: warns only when the old argument name is passed
@deprecated(target=TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, args_mapping={"val": "new_val"}, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def renamed_arg(val: int = 0, new_val: int = 0) -> int:
    return new_val


going_away(1)  # warns: FutureWarning — "going_away was deprecated since v1.0 …"
renamed_arg(new_val=1)  # silent — new name used, no deprecated arg present
renamed_arg(val=1)  # warns: FutureWarning — "renamed_arg uses deprecated arguments: `val` → `new_val` …"

target=True (or TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP) without args_mapping is a misconfiguration. Since v0.8, target=True is a deprecated sentinel for TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP. Using either without args_mapping emits construction-time warnings:

  • The legacy sentinel emits a FutureWarning.
  • ARGS_REMAP emits a UserWarning because it requires args_mapping to have any effect.

This will become a TypeError in v1.0. If your intent is to warn callers with no forwarding or remapping, use TargetMode.NOTIFY instead.

docs.title: Stacked deprecation decorators
docs.text:
Stack multiple @deprecated decorators on a single function to handle migrations that span several releases. Each layer tracks its own version range and warning count independently.

Not all stacking combinations are supported. Only three combinations work correctly. Everything else emits UserWarning at decoration time (not at call time) so you catch the misconfiguration immediately. See the supported combinations table below.

docs.title: Pattern 1 — multi-step argument renames (ARGS_REMAP + ARGS_REMAP)
docs.text:
When an argument is renamed more than once across releases, stack one @deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, ...) per rename. Each decorator operates on its own version range and emits a separate notice, giving callers version-specific migration guidance.

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated


@deprecated(
    TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP,
    deprecated_in="0.3",
    remove_in="0.6",
    args_mapping=dict(c1="nc1"),
    message_template="Depr: v%(deprecated_in)s rm v%(remove_in)s for args: %(argument_map)s.",
)
@deprecated(
    TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP,
    deprecated_in="0.4",
    remove_in="0.7",
    args_mapping=dict(nc1="nc2"),
    message_template="Depr: v%(deprecated_in)s rm v%(remove_in)s for args: %(argument_map)s.",
)
def any_pow(base, c1: float = 0, nc1: float = 0, nc2: float = 2) -> float:
    return base**nc2


# calling this function will raise deprecation warnings:
#   FutureWarning('Depr: v0.3 rm v0.6 for args: `c1` -> `nc1`.')
#   FutureWarning('Depr: v0.4 rm v0.7 for args: `nc1` -> `nc2`.')
print(any_pow(2, 3))
Output: any_pow(2, 3) 
8

docs.title: Pattern 2 — lifecycle migration (ARGS_REMAP + NOTIFY)
docs.text:
The most common real-world lifecycle has two stages:

  1. An argument is renamed in an early release (ARGS_REMAP).
  2. The entire function is deprecated in a later release once a complete replacement exists (NOTIFY).

Put ARGS_REMAP outermost (top decorator) and NOTIFY below it.

Callers still using the old argument name receive both warnings — the arg-rename notice and the function-deprecated notice. Callers already using the new name receive only the function-deprecated notice.

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated


@deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0", args_mapping={"factor": "scale"})
@deprecated(TargetMode.NOTIFY, deprecated_in="2.0", remove_in="3.0")
def compute_power(base: float, factor: float = 1, scale: float = 1) -> float:
    return base**scale


print(compute_power(2, factor=3))  # → 2 warnings (arg rename + function deprecated)
print(compute_power(2, scale=3))  # → 1 warning  (function deprecated only)
Output: compute_power(2, factor=3); compute_power(2, scale=3) 
8
8

Wrong order raises UserWarning at decoration time. @deprecated(NOTIFY) on top of @deprecated(ARGS_REMAP) is the wrong order — pyDeprecate detects it and warns immediately at decoration time with the message "Reverse the decorator order: put @deprecated(ARGS_REMAP, ...) outermost".

docs.title: Supported stacking combinations
docs.text:
Outer (top) Inner (bottom) Status Notes ARGS_REMAP ARGS_REMAP ✅ Multi-step argument renames across versions ARGS_REMAP NOTIFY ✅ Lifecycle: rename args first, then deprecate the whole function NOTIFY callable ✅ Outer NOTIFY warns callers the function is going away; inner callable handles forwarding. Prefer @deprecated(target=<callable>) directly — same effect, simpler. callable callable ❌ Use a single @deprecated(target=<callable>) instead callable ARGS_REMAP ❌ Collapse to @deprecated(target=fn, args_mapping={...}) callable NOTIFY ❌ Collapse to a single @deprecated(target=<callable>) ARGS_REMAP callable ❌ Update the inner decorator to include both target= and args_mapping= NOTIFY NOTIFY ❌ Update the existing decorator's versions instead of adding a second one NOTIFY ARGS_REMAP ❌ Wrong order — swap: ARGS_REMAP on top, NOTIFY below

✅ = supported ❌ = unsupported — emits UserWarning at decoration time

docs.title: N-level stacking
docs.text:
Any sequence of supported adjacent pairs stacks transitively. The guard inspects only one hop at a time — as long as each adjacent pair is a supported combination, the full stack is accepted silently.

Example — three-level lifecycle migration:

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated


@deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, deprecated_in="0.3", remove_in="0.6", args_mapping={"c1": "nc1"})
@deprecated(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, deprecated_in="0.4", remove_in="0.7", args_mapping={"nc1": "nc2"})
@deprecated(TargetMode.NOTIFY, deprecated_in="0.7", remove_in="1.0")
def any_pow(base, c1: float = 0, nc1: float = 0, nc2: float = 2) -> float:
    return base**nc2


print(any_pow(2))
Output: any_pow(2) 
4

Each adjacent pair is ARGS_REMAP + ARGS_REMAP (supported) and ARGS_REMAP + NOTIFY (supported), so no decoration-time warning fires. The three layers execute in turn at call time.

Unsupported pair breaks the whole chain. A single unsupported adjacent pair anywhere in the stack emits UserWarning at decoration time for that pair. Chains with NOTIFY + ARGS_REMAP adjacent remain unsupported — the wrong-order warning still fires.

Use validate_deprecation_chains() in CI to catch accidental deprecated-to-deprecated chains automatically.

docs.title: Conditional skip
docs.text:
skip_if accepts a boolean or a zero-argument callable returning a boolean. When it evaluates to True, the deprecation notice is suppressed and the call proceeds normally.

This is useful when behaviour depends on runtime conditions, for example suppressing the notice once the caller has migrated to a newer dependency. skip_if is available on @deprecated, deprecated_callable(), and the class/instance proxies; see Classes.

from deprecate import TargetMode, deprecated_callable

FAKE_VERSION = 1


def version_greater_1():
    return FAKE_VERSION > 1


@deprecated_callable(TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP, "0.3", "0.6", args_mapping=dict(c1="nc1"), skip_if=version_greater_1)
def skip_pow(base, c1: float = 1, nc1: float = 1) -> float:
    return base ** (c1 - nc1)


# calling this function will raise a deprecation warning
print(skip_pow(2, 3))

# change the fake versions
FAKE_VERSION = 2

# will not raise any warning
print(skip_pow(2, 3))
Output: skip_pow(2, 3) 
0.25
4

docs.title: Fatal deprecations
docs.text:
as_exception=True raises DeprecatedError instead of emitting the warning, carrying the same rendered message. The call is refused: the forwarding target is never invoked and the source body never runs. TargetMode.NOTIFY and TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP therefore stop instead of falling through to the body.

This is the middle step of the warn → raise → delete lifecycle. It is available on every entry point: @deprecated, deprecated_callable(), deprecated_class(), deprecated_instance(), and deprecated_module().

num_warns does not apply in fatal mode. A fatal deprecation raises on every call. A budget would stop refusing after the first attempt, allowing a caller retrying inside except to sail through.

stream=None silences the message, not the raise. Fatal mode is a lifecycle state, not an output channel.

skip_if still suppresses everything, fatal deprecations included — a wrapper switched off by configuration is not a deprecation at that moment.

from deprecate import DeprecatedError, TargetMode, deprecated_callable


@deprecated_callable(TargetMode.NOTIFY, "1.0", "2.0", as_exception=True)
def legacy_checksum(payload: str) -> int:
    return len(payload)


try:
    legacy_checksum("abc")
except DeprecatedError as err:
    print(err)

# the call is refused again: the `num_warns` budget does not apply to a fatal deprecation
try:
    legacy_checksum("again")
except DeprecatedError as err:
    print(type(err).__name__)
Output: legacy_checksum("abc"); legacy_checksum("again") 
The `legacy_checksum` was deprecated since v1.0. It will be removed in v2.0.
DeprecatedError

docs.title: The global switch
docs.text:
deprecate.AS_EXCEPTIONS is the process-wide default, seeded at import from the DEPRECATE_AS_EXCEPTIONS environment variable. Values 1, true, yes, or on enable it; anything else is off.

It is re-read on every emission. An application can flip it during bootstrap and a test suite can toggle it per case:

DEPRECATE_AS_EXCEPTIONS=1 pytest

To make deprecations fatal for one stretch of code only, use the as_exceptions() context manager. Deprecations that defer to the global switch raise inside the block. The previous setting applies again on exit, including when the block raises, so nested scopes compose.

as_exceptions(False) does the reverse and exempts a block from a strict run. It also works as a decorator.

from deprecate import DeprecatedError, as_exceptions, deprecated


# NEW API — replacement that calculates the total
def calculate_total(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — `legacy_total` now forwards to `calculate_total`
@deprecated(
    target=calculate_total,
    deprecated_in="1.0",
    remove_in="2.0",
    message_template="Use `calculate_total` instead.",
    num_warns=-1,
)
def legacy_total(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    pass


try:
    with as_exceptions():
        legacy_total(1, 2)
except DeprecatedError as err:
    print(err)

with as_exceptions(False):  # exempt this call, so the output holds even under DEPRECATE_AS_EXCEPTIONS=1
    print(legacy_total(1, 2))  # warns: FutureWarning
Output: legacy_total(1, 2) in the strict block, then in the exempt block 
Use `calculate_total` instead.
3

The scope is held in a ContextVar, local to the current thread and asyncio task. Other threads and sibling tasks keep the global setting, and holding a scope across an await is safe.

Tasks created inside the block inherit the scope, because a task copies the context when it is created. Whether a new thread inherits it depends on the interpreter:

  • A new thread inherits the scope only when the interpreter copies the starting context into it. That is sys.flags.thread_inherit_context on Python 3.14+: on by default in free-threaded builds, opt-in with -X thread_inherit_context=1 otherwise.
  • An inheriting thread, including a pool worker started inside the scope, keeps the scope after the block closes.
  • Otherwise, asyncio.to_thread carries the scope into a thread by default.
  • Any other thread inherits it only through explicit propagation: contextvars.copy_context().run(...), or threading.Thread(context=...) on Python 3.14+.
  • loop.run_in_executor does not propagate context per call. A worker started outside the scope sees the global setting; an inheriting worker started inside it retains that scope.

Run the thread's target through contextvars.copy_context().run(...) when it must inherit the scope.

The scope never modifies deprecate.AS_EXCEPTIONS. Inside the block that attribute still reports the global value, and assigning it there takes effect once the block closes.

Scope and decorator limits

A generator or async generator shares its consumer's context. A scope held across a yield also applies to the consumer while the generator is suspended. Open and close the scope within one step of the generator; see Limitations.

As a decorator it only covers plain synchronous functions. Decorating an async def, generator or async-generator function raises TypeError, because its body would run after the scope closed. Use with as_exceptions(): inside the body instead.

A non-bool flag, including a bare @as_exceptions without parentheses, raises TypeError at the call.

Like deprecate.AS_EXCEPTIONS itself, it is the consumer's switch: an application or test suite. Library code should not use as_exceptions(False) to escape a caller's strict run.

Precedence is monotonic: an explicit as_exception=True is always fatal. as_exception=False means "not fatal by default" but still yields to a True global.

A wrapper's own as_exception=False therefore cannot opt a consumer's strict run out. Only the consumer's own as_exceptions(False) scope or AS_EXCEPTIONS setting can do that. An author can still promote one symbol ahead of the rest.

docs.title: Recipe: the warning becomes an error at version X
docs.text:
To promote a deprecation from warning to error on a schedule, compute as_exception from your package version and a version of your choosing. Here that version is ERROR_IN, typically between deprecated_in and remove_in. as_exception is read once, at decoration time, so the switch flips on the first import under the new version.

Compare parsed versions rather than strings. Tuples below keep the example dependency-free; packaging.version.Version works the same.

from deprecate import DeprecatedError, TargetMode, deprecated_callable

PACKAGE_VERSION = (1, 3)  # in a real package: parse your own `__version__`
ERROR_IN = (1, 3)  # the release where callers must stop using the old name


@deprecated_callable(TargetMode.NOTIFY, "1.0", "2.0", as_exception=PACKAGE_VERSION >= ERROR_IN)
def legacy_digest(payload: str) -> int:
    return len(payload)


try:
    legacy_digest("abc")
except DeprecatedError as err:
    print(err)
Output: legacy_digest("abc") 
The `legacy_digest` was deprecated since v1.0. It will be removed in v2.0.

Below ERROR_IN the same code only warns. As the release-time backstop, run pydeprecate expiry in CI. It exits 1 when any wrapper is past its remove_in deadline, so a deprecation that was never deleted cannot ship by accident.

docs.title: When to prefer -W error instead
docs.text:
Python already turns warnings into exceptions: -W error::FutureWarning or PYTHONWARNINGS=error::FutureWarning. Use those when you want every library's FutureWarning to raise. as_exception exists for the three cases they cannot cover:

  1. Scope — fail only on pyDeprecate's own deprecations, not on NumPy's or pandas'.
  2. Non-warnings streams — a wrapper with stream=logging.warning never reaches the warnings machinery, so no filter can make it fail.
  3. Per-symbol promotion — ship one deprecation as fatal while the rest keep warning.

docs.title: Strict callable-only deprecation
docs.text:
@deprecated dispatches a class source to @deprecated_class(). @deprecated_callable() is the strict form: it shares every @deprecated parameter but raises TypeError at decoration time when applied to a class. A mistaken class decoration then fails on import instead of silently becoming a proxy.

Use it where the class path should never be taken implicitly:

  • shared library code;
  • internal helpers that only wrap functions;
  • modules whose reviewers want the class case to be an error.
from deprecate import deprecated_callable


# NEW API — renamed to say what it measures
def elapsed_seconds(start: float, end: float) -> float:
    return end - start


# DEPRECATED API — `duration` was the original name before the rename
@deprecated_callable(target=elapsed_seconds, deprecated_in="1.4", remove_in="2.0")
def duration(start: float, end: float) -> float: ...


print(duration(10.0, 12.5))  # warns: FutureWarning
Output: duration(10.0, 12.5) 
2.5

Applied to a class, it refuses at decoration time:

from deprecate import deprecated_callable


class HttpClient:
    """The replacement class."""


try:

    @deprecated_callable(target=HttpClient, deprecated_in="1.4", remove_in="2.0")
    class Client:
        """A class handed to the strict callable-only decorator."""

except TypeError as err:
    print(type(err).__name__)
Output: type(err).__name__ 
TypeError

The error names both alternatives: @deprecated_class() for the class itself, or @deprecated for automatic dispatch.

Different target defaults. @deprecated defaults target to TargetMode.AUTO, inferred at decoration time. deprecated_callable() defaults to TargetMode.NOTIFY and rejects an explicit TargetMode.AUTO with TypeError.

docs.title: Static type checkers (PEP 702)
docs.text:
mypy, pyright, and IDEs flag a deprecated symbol only when its decorator is literally warnings.deprecated (Python 3.13+) or its backport typing_extensions.deprecated. They recognise the decorator by name, not by what it does at runtime. @deprecated from pyDeprecate is invisible to them.

To get the strikethrough in the editor and pyDeprecate's forwarding and warning, stack the PEP 702 decorator directly above pyDeprecate's:

import typing_extensions  # on Python 3.13+: `import warnings` and `@warnings.deprecated(...)`

from deprecate import deprecated


# NEW API — the renamed helper
def fetch_orders(customer_id: int) -> list:
    return [customer_id]


# DEPRECATED API — struck through by type checkers, forwarded with a warning at runtime
@typing_extensions.deprecated("Use `fetch_orders` instead.", category=None)
@deprecated(target=fetch_orders, deprecated_in="1.4", remove_in="2.0")
def get_orders(customer_id: int) -> list: ...


print(get_orders(7))  # warns: FutureWarning
Output: get_orders(7) 
[7]

Four rules make the pair work:

Rule Reason or placement Set category=None. The PEP 702 decorator then only marks the symbol for type checkers. Otherwise every call emits a second DeprecationWarning next to pyDeprecate's FutureWarning. Use a string-literal message. mypy silently ignores a message held in a constant or built with an f-string. pyright still flags the symbol but drops the text. Place it directly above @deprecated(...). Keep it inside @staticmethod / @classmethod, and above the outer-order @deprecated(...) @property. mypy asks for # type: ignore[prop-decorator] on that line, as it does for any decorator above @property. Placed under @property, pyright misses it. Import the module, not the name. from typing_extensions import deprecated shadows pyDeprecate's deprecated. Write @typing_extensions.deprecated(...) or @warnings.deprecated(...).

IDEs strike the symbol through as soon as the decorator is there. To fail CI on new uses, turn the diagnostic into an error — mypy leaves it off by default:

[tool.mypy]
enable_error_code = ["deprecated"]

[tool.pyright]
reportDeprecated = "error"

Since v0.14, @deprecated and deprecated_callable() keep the decorated callable's own type, and the package ships a py.typed marker. Type checkers therefore see the real signature and name the symbol correctly in the diagnostic.

For class aliases see Classes → Type annotations and static analysis. To list symbols deprecated with the PEP 702 decorator alone, see include_pep702.

Static types vs runtime

That static type is the source's type. Decorating a functools.lru_cache / functools.cache object returns a plain function. cache_clear() and cache_info() are gone even though type checkers still offer them.

Deprecate the underlying function and put the cache on top (@functools.lru_cache above @deprecated(...)). The cache attributes then exist, but a cache hit never reaches the wrapper. The warning therefore fires only on a miss.

A functools.partial is rejected at decoration time; wrap it in a plain def and decorate that. Other callable objects without a __name__ are rejected too; wrap those with deprecated_instance().

docs.title: Deprecation lifecycle
docs.text: Follow a summation API from its deprecation in 0.1 to removal in 0.5.

docs.title: 1. Add the wrapper
docs.text:
Keep the old entry point while forwarding calls to its replacement.

from deprecate import deprecated, void


# NEW API — adds quantities using the replacement implementation
def base_sum_kwargs(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — `decorated_sum` replaced by `base_sum_kwargs`
@deprecated(target=base_sum_kwargs, deprecated_in="0.1", remove_in="0.5")
def decorated_sum(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    """Add two quantities through the compatibility entry point."""
    return void(a, b)


print(decorated_sum(2, 3))  # warns: FutureWarning
Output: decorated_sum(2, 3) 
5

This forwards the compatibility function to the replacement. See Functions for forwarding and argument mapping, or Classes for class migrations.

docs.title: 2. Warn callers
docs.text:
The default FutureWarning names the deprecated function, replacement, introduction version, and removal version. The summation call still returns the replacement's result.

num_warns Behavior 1 (default) Emit once per wrapper lifetime. N > 1 Emit at most N times per wrapper lifetime. -1 Emit on every call. 0 Suppress deprecation messages.

For argument deprecations, the warning budget applies per deprecated argument.

Python's warning filters can further limit visible warnings. Set stream to a logger or another callable to redirect messages, or None to silence them. Forwarding still works with stream=None.

See Customization for message templates and stream signatures.

docs.title: 3. Test the migration
docs.text:
Check both the compatibility result and the replacement's warning-free behavior.

import pytest

from deprecate import assert_no_warnings, deprecated


# NEW API — adds quantities without a deprecation notice
def base_sum_kwargs(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — give the compatibility function an independent warning budget
@deprecated(target=base_sum_kwargs, deprecated_in="0.1", remove_in="0.5")
def decorated_sum(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    return a + b


def test_summation_migration() -> None:
    """Keep legacy callers working while new callers use the replacement.

    A consumer still calls the compatibility entry point during the migration
    window. It must warn once, return the correct total, and then stay silent.
    """
    with pytest.warns(FutureWarning, match="base_sum_kwargs"):
        assert decorated_sum(2, 3) == 5
    with assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning):
        assert base_sum_kwargs(2, 3) == 5
        assert decorated_sum(2, 3) == 5


test_summation_migration()
print("Migration checks passed.")
Output: test_summation_migration() 
Migration checks passed.

See Testing for pytest patterns, warning budgets, and assert_no_warnings message matching.

docs.title: 4. Audit in CI
docs.text:
Run the same audits locally and in CI before each release.

  1. Install pyDeprecate[audit] in the audit environment.
  2. Run pydeprecate expiry --version 0.4 <package-path> while the summation wrapper is still supported.
  3. Run pydeprecate policy <package-path> to enforce your configured grace period and metadata requirements.
  4. Configure pre-commit hooks or the GitHub Action to repeat the checks automatically.

Replace <package-path> with your package's source path. See CLI Reference for arguments and exit codes, and CI Integration for pre-commit and Action recipes.

Confirm audit coverage

Review skipped imports and version-detection gaps. Pass --version explicitly when the package version cannot be detected. A passing scan does not prove that skipped modules were checked.

docs.title: 5. Remove and prune
docs.text:
At version 0.5, the expiry gate reports the summation wrapper because the current version has reached remove_in.

  1. Run pydeprecate expiry --version 0.5 <package-path> to identify wrappers due for removal.
  2. Delete decorated_sum and remove the old name from public re-exports and import lists.
  3. Migrate remaining internal callers to base_sum_kwargs.
  4. Prune obsolete compatibility tests, documentation examples, and wrapper-only imports.
  5. Keep replacement tests, regenerate the deprecation table, and rerun the audits.

Removal is manual

remove_in records a deadline. It does not delete the wrapper or automatically stop forwarding calls. The expiry gate fails for expired wrappers unless failure is explicitly suppressed with --exit-zero.

docs.title: 6. Record the release
docs.text:
Generate the active deprecation inventory before removing wrappers, so release notes can preserve their migration information.

from types import ModuleType
from deprecate import deprecated, generate_deprecation_table


# NEW API — the replacement adds quantities
def base_sum_kwargs(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    return a + b


# DEPRECATED API — the old name remains discoverable until removal
@deprecated(target=base_sum_kwargs, deprecated_in="0.1", remove_in="0.5")
def decorated_sum(a: int, b: int = 5) -> int:
    return a + b


module = ModuleType("example")
module.decorated_sum = decorated_sum
report = generate_deprecation_table(module, current_version="0.4", recursive=False)
print("Deprecation Active" in report)
Output: Deprecation Active in report 
True

generate_deprecation_table returns Markdown from discovered wrapper metadata. See Audit Tools for the full table and style="matrix" release columns.

  1. Announce the deprecation, replacement, and planned removal version when introducing the wrapper.
  2. Record the removed public name and replacement in the removal release's changelog and release notes.
  3. Publish the refreshed inventory after deletion; removed wrappers no longer appear in a live scan.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
deprecated_module() marks an entire Python module as deprecated by replacing its __class__ with an intercepting wrapper. Every public attribute access on the old module name invokes its FutureWarning path. Standard warning filters can suppress repeated display.

Three patterns are supported:

  • Mode 1 warns in place without moving any code.
  • Mode 2 redirects attribute access to a replacement module.
  • Mode 3 exposes a deprecated module name as a package attribute.

For deprecating individual functions see Functions; for classes see Classes.

docs.title: When to use deprecated_module()
docs.text:
Reach for deprecated_module() when a module is being replaced or renamed. Every attribute access on the old name invokes the configured warning path automatically.

Place the call at the bottom of the file being deprecated. It reassigns the module's __class__ to an intercepting wrapper and attaches __deprecation_config__ metadata. This lets find_deprecation_wrappers() discover it.

docs.title: Mode 1 — in-place warn
docs.text:
Use this when you want to keep the module in place and invoke its warning path on every attribute access. Call deprecated_module(__name__, ...) at the bottom of old_calculator.py:

# phmdoctest:skip — old_calculator.py in-place warn template
# old_calculator.py — DEPRECATED API; use new_calculator instead
# NEW API — same functions now live in new_calculator.py

from deprecate import deprecated_module


def add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Add two numbers. Prefer new_calculator.add."""
    return a + b


def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Multiply two numbers. Prefer new_calculator.multiply."""
    return a * b


# Mark this module deprecated — call once at the bottom.
# name is optional; when omitted it is auto-detected from the caller's __name__.
# Without message_template, the warning reads:
#   FutureWarning: The `old_calculator` module was deprecated since v2.0. It will be removed in v3.0.
# With message_template (as below), it replaces the built-in notice entirely:
#   FutureWarning: Use `new_calculator` instead.
deprecated_module(
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
    message_template="Use `new_calculator` instead.",
)

import old_calculator; old_calculator.add(1, 2) invokes the FutureWarning path and returns the result. Every public attribute access — real functions, classes, constants — takes that path because deprecated_module() replaces the module's __class__ with an intercepting wrapper. Standard filters can suppress repeated display.

attrs_mapping also works here without a target. {"old_name": "new_name"} serves the module's own new_name for old_name, even when old_name still exists in the module, and {"gone": None} makes gone raise AttributeError. Use it to rename or remove a module attribute in place.

Call it at module top level when omitting name. Auto-detection reads the caller frame's __name__. This only names the intended module when the call sits directly in the module body. Calling without name from a function or class body (e.g. a _setup_deprecations() helper) raises TypeError. The frame's __name__ would point at the enclosing module and silently deprecate all of it. Pass name explicitly to call from any other scope.

docs.title: Mode 2 — redirect to a replacement module
docs.text:
Use this when you rename an entire module. Attribute lookups missing from the old module's __dict__ are forwarded to new_calculator, so callers get both a warning and the correct value. Real attributes already defined in the old module (functions, constants) are served from its __dict__ directly; they warn but are not forwarded.

Redirect cycle detection uses context-local state and restores the prior state when the outer lookup finishes. Cyclic redirects raise AttributeError rather than recursing indefinitely. Contexts copied during a lookup can resolve the same name again after that lookup finishes. This applies whether it returned a value or raised an exception.

# phmdoctest:skip — CI template; new_calculator is not installed
# old_calculator.py — DEPRECATED API — redirect to new_calculator
# NEW API — same functions live in new_calculator.py

from deprecate import deprecated_module

# Load the replacement module to attach as redirect target
import new_calculator as _new_calculator


deprecated_module(
    __name__,
    target=_new_calculator,  # every unknown attr forwarded here
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
    message_template="Use `new_calculator` instead.",
)

Now import old_calculator; old_calculator.add(1, 2) invokes the FutureWarning path and returns the result from new_calculator.add; standard warning filters can suppress repeated display. The attrs_mapping parameter lets you rename specific attributes during the redirect:

# phmdoctest:skip — attrs_mapping continuation; requires new_calculator
# Map old attr name to new attr name, or to None to raise AttributeError.
# Keys are the names callers use today (the original API names).
from deprecate import deprecated_module

deprecated_module(
    __name__,
    target=_new_calculator,
    attrs_mapping={"compute": "add", "beta_feature": None},
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
)

old_calculator.compute invokes the warning path and forwards to new_calculator.add (the function was renamed). old_calculator.beta_feature invokes it and raises AttributeError (no replacement). Standard filters can suppress repeated display; all other names fall through to new_calculator.

docs.title: Mode 3 — parent alias via deprecated_instance
docs.text:
When reorganising a package, use deprecated_instance() in the parent __init__.py to keep the old sub-module name accessible as a parent-package attribute. This does not require a new API; it reuses the existing proxy mechanism.

# phmdoctest:skip — CI template; my_package is not installed
# my_package/__init__.py

import my_package.new_calculator as _new_calculator
from deprecate import deprecated_instance

# DEPRECATED API — expose `old_utils` as a package attribute pointing to new_calculator
old_utils = deprecated_instance(
    _new_calculator,
    name="old_utils",
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
    message_template="Use `my_package.new_calculator` instead.",
)

import my_package; my_package.old_utils.add(1, 2) invokes the FutureWarning path on the first attribute access and forwards to new_calculator; standard filters can suppress display.

docs.title: Limiting warning volume with num_warns
docs.text:
By default deprecated_module() delivers a warning on every public attribute access, matching its behavior before num_warns existed. Standard warning filters can still suppress repeated display at the same location.

Pass num_warns to cap deliveries with the same semantics as @deprecated's num_warns. The default is -1 (unlimited) instead of 1 until v1.0. It then becomes 1 like everywhere else (see the box below).

# phmdoctest:skip — old_calculator.py in-place warn template, budgeted variant
from deprecate import deprecated_module

deprecated_module(
    deprecated_in="2.0",
    remove_in="3.0",
    num_warns=1,  # warn once per process, then stay silent
)
num_warns Deliveries 0 It never delivers a warning. A positive N It delivers exactly N warnings. -1 (the default) It delivers on every access.

The counter is one budget shared across every attribute name on the module. There is no per-attribute counter the way deprecated_class's attrs_mapping gets one.

-1 avoids budget locking but still performs metadata lookup and warning handling. Use a finite budget for a worker service whose custom stream or warning filter would otherwise record repeated accesses.

Changes in v1.0

Omit stream to deliver the module warning through warnings.warn (the default; help(deprecated_module) shows it as <warnings.warn>). An explicit stream=None does the same today, but emits a FutureWarning at the deprecated_module(...) call.

In v1.0 stream=None will silence the module warning, as it already does for @deprecated, deprecated_class and deprecated_instance. In the same release the num_warns default changes from -1 to 1. Pass num_warns=-1 explicitly to keep a warning on every access.

A missing deprecated_in warns at install time. deprecated_module emits a UserWarning ("has no deprecated_in set") when deprecated_in is empty. A message_template silences it, as for @deprecated, deprecated_class and deprecated_instance; stream=None does not yet, because the module keeps delivering its warning until v1.0. Otherwise pass deprecated_in.

docs.title: Existing module hooks and repeat calls
docs.text:
The install itself can emit three more UserWarning notices:

  • Existing __getattr__. A module that already defines a PEP 562 __getattr__ keeps it: lookups the wrapper cannot serve are chained to it, and the install warns that it is chaining.
  • Repeat call. An identical repeat call is silent. A repeat with a different configuration is ignored with a warning, and the original configuration stays.
  • Custom __class__. A module whose __class__ is already custom, for example one installed by a lazy loader, is overwritten with the wrapper and its prior behaviour is lost; the install warns about it.

docs.title: Star imports also warn
docs.text:
Star imports (from old_calculator import *) still trigger the deprecation warning. CPython's IMPORT_STAR bytecode calls getattr(module, name) for each public name being pulled in. That call routes through the same __getattribute__ interception installed by deprecated_module().

A FutureWarning therefore fires once per pulled-in public name, exactly as it would for old_calculator.add(1, 2). A PEP 562 module-level __getattr__ hook fires only for missing names. Star imports can invoke it for dynamic names listed in __all__, but not for existing attributes.

docs.title: Audit integration
docs.text:
find_deprecation_wrappers() discovers modules marked with deprecated_module() the same way it discovers function and class wrappers — by reading the __deprecation_config__ attribute attached to the module object:

# phmdoctest:skip — CI template: replace my_package with your actual package
import my_package
from deprecate import find_deprecation_wrappers

deprecated_items = find_deprecation_wrappers(my_package)
module_items = [r for r in deprecated_items if r.api_type == "module"]

docs.title: Fatal deprecations
docs.text:
deprecated_module(..., as_exception=True) turns every public attribute access on the module into a raised DeprecatedError — see Fatal deprecations for the full contract, including the process-wide DEPRECATE_AS_EXCEPTIONS switch. It ignores num_warns (every access raises, not just the first) and does not depend on stream.

Tools that walk module attributes

A module is the broadest surface this feature covers, so expect the blast radius to match. Tools that walk module attributes stop at a fatal module rather than skipping it. This includes pytest collection, Sphinx autodoc, pickle, and copy.

pyDeprecate's own audit is unaffected. find_deprecation_wrappers() and the pydeprecate CLI read the module's __dict__ rather than going through attribute access. A fatal module therefore still appears in discovery and reports like any other.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: This page covers deprecation of @property and @cached_property descriptors: decorator order rules, all-accessor wrapping, setter/deleter chains, and the dataclass field alias pattern. For function deprecation see Functions; for class deprecation see Classes.

docs.title: Properties and cached properties
docs.text:
@deprecated works with @property and @cached_property. The decorator only adds a FutureWarning at access time; it does not forward reads or writes to another property.

Order Accessors that warn Outer: @deprecated @property, or explicit deprecated(...)(property(fget, fset, fdel)) All three accessors (fget, fset, fdel) warn on read, write, and delete. Inner-first: @property @deprecated Only fget warns; apply @deprecated to setter and deleter separately if they must also warn.

For a getter-only property both orders warn on read, but use the outer order: the inner order @property @deprecated fails pydeprecate check.

from functools import cached_property

from deprecate import deprecated


class Config:
    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    @property
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        return 30

    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    @cached_property
    def base_url(self) -> str:
        return "https://example.com"


print(Config().timeout)
Output: Config().timeout 
30

The FutureWarning fires on attribute access (obj.timeout), not on a call.

Cached properties warn on first access only

For @cached_property, subsequent accesses return the cached value without emitting another warning. The cache is filled after the first read. While that value remains cached, later reads of the same object do not reach pyDeprecate. Deleting the cached attribute makes the next read invoke the descriptor again, which can warn when the budget allows.

  • With num_warns=-1, each new object warns once, on its first access.
  • The default num_warns=1 budget is shared by all objects, so only the first object to read the property warns.

Decorator order for getter-only properties. Use @deprecated @property (outer) order. The inner order @property @deprecated also warns on read for a getter-only property, but pydeprecate check and find_deprecation_wrappers flag it, because a later setter or deleter would be silently unprotected. For properties with a setter or deleter, outer order is required; see the next section.

docs.title: Deprecating a property with a setter or deleter
docs.text:
When the property being deprecated has a setter or deleter, all three accessors (fget, fset, fdel) are wrapped automatically — each fires a FutureWarning. Both the chain-style decorator pattern and the explicit construction pattern work:

from deprecate import deprecated


class Config:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._timeout: int = 30

    # Outer order required: @deprecated @property wraps fget, fset, and fdel
    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    @property
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        return self._timeout

    @timeout.setter
    def timeout(self, value: int) -> None:
        self._timeout = value

    @timeout.deleter
    def timeout(self) -> None:
        del self._timeout


cfg = Config()
cfg.timeout = 10  # FutureWarning: write
print(cfg.timeout)  # FutureWarning: read; prints 10
del cfg.timeout  # FutureWarning: delete
Output: cfg.timeout 
10

obj.timeout fires FutureWarning on read, obj.timeout = value fires on write, and del obj.timeout fires on delete.

Per-accessor warnings

To warn on the getter only, apply @deprecated directly to fget using inner order (@property @deprecated) instead of wrapping the full property object; the setter and deleter then remain silent. pydeprecate check flags that shape, so it suits only code you do not audit.

Each accessor (fget, fset, fdel) has its own warning counter — assert read, write, and delete warnings in separate pytest.warns blocks, or use num_warns=-1 to disable per-accessor deduplication.

The explicit property(fget, fset[, fdel]) construction also works:

from deprecate import deprecated


def _timeout_fget(self) -> int:
    return self._timeout


def _timeout_fset(self, value: int) -> None:
    self._timeout = value


def _timeout_fdel(self) -> None:
    del self._timeout


class Config:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._timeout: int = 30

    timeout = deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")(property(_timeout_fget, _timeout_fset, _timeout_fdel))

find_deprecation_wrappers discovers explicit-construction properties via the accessor that carries __deprecation_config__ metadata. For setter-only properties (property(None, fset)), it discovers via fset; if fget is plain (not deprecated), it falls through to fset or fdel.

docs.title: Strict mode: from deprecate import property
docs.text:
The inner order @property @deprecated wraps only fget. If you later add a setter or deleter with @value.setter / @value.deleter, those accessors are rebuilt from the plain property base. They are silently unprotected: writes and deletes never warn.

This is easy to introduce by habit, because the standard library puts @property outermost.

To catch this at definition time, import the strict property replacement. It raises TypeError the moment a getter already carrying @deprecated metadata is handed to it — before any instance is created:

# phmdoctest:skip — TypeError raised at class-body time
from deprecate import deprecated, property  # `property` shadows the builtin in this module only


class Config:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._timeout: int = 30

    # ! Raises TypeError at class-body evaluation time — inner order detected
    @property
    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        return self._timeout

The fix is to switch to the canonical outer order @deprecated(...) @property, which wraps every accessor and survives later setter/deleter additions. The outer order works unchanged with the strict property:

from deprecate import deprecated, property


class Config:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._timeout: int = 30

    # NEW: outer order — strict `property` passes through, all accessors warn
    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    @property
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        return self._timeout

The strict property is a subclass of the builtin, so isinstance(obj, property) checks and the audit scanner treat it transparently. Importing it shadows the builtin only in the importing module — modules that do not import it keep the builtin behaviour, so the strictness is purely opt-in.

Auditing existing code: the inner_order_property flag

Even without the strict import, find_deprecation_wrappers flags every inner-order @property. Each DeprecationWrapperInfo carries inner_order_property=True when the wrapper is a plain property whose fget is deprecation-wrapped. The flag fires for the getter-only shape too, because the canonical form is the outer order.

CI pipelines can reject any result with this flag set to eliminate the silent write/delete gap across a whole package. See the Audit guide for the full CI integration pattern.

docs.title: Deprecated property alias on a dataclass
docs.text:
When a dataclass field is renamed, define a property with the old name that delegates to the new field in its accessor body. @deprecated adds a FutureWarning to each accessor — the delegation itself is plain Python in the method body, not something the library provides.

Read-only alias (warns on read only):

from dataclasses import dataclass

from deprecate import deprecated


@dataclass
class Config:
    timeout_ms: int = 30_000  # renamed from `timeout`

    @property
    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        """Deprecated — use ``timeout_ms`` instead."""
        return self.timeout_ms // 1000


cfg = Config(timeout_ms=5_000)
print(cfg.timeout)  # FutureWarning fired; prints 5
Output: cfg.timeout 
5

Read-write alias (warns on read and write): use the outer order and chain .setter:

from dataclasses import dataclass

from deprecate import deprecated


@dataclass
class Config:
    timeout_ms: int = 30_000  # renamed from `timeout`

    @deprecated(deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
    @property
    def timeout(self) -> int:
        return self.timeout_ms // 1000

    @timeout.setter
    def timeout(self, value: int) -> None:
        self.timeout_ms = value * 1000


cfg = Config(timeout_ms=5_000)
print(cfg.timeout)  # FutureWarning fired; prints 5
cfg.timeout = 10  # FutureWarning fired; sets timeout_ms = 10_000
print(cfg.timeout_ms)  # prints 10_000
Output: cfg.timeout; cfg.timeout_ms 
5
10000

cfg.timeout fires FutureWarning (from @deprecated) and the getter body returns cfg.timeout_ms // 1000. cfg.timeout = 5 fires FutureWarning and the setter body assigns cfg.timeout_ms = 5000.

Do not shadow a dataclass field

Do not use the same name as an existing dataclass field for the deprecated property. The @dataclass-generated __init__ performs self.field = value, which conflicts with a property descriptor of the same name. Use a different name for the deprecated alias and keep the dataclass field under its new name.

The same pattern works on regular (non-dataclass) classes — replace field access with self._attr lookups in the accessor body. @deprecated only adds the warning in either case.

@deprecated rejects target=<callable>, args_mapping, args_extra, TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP / True and TargetMode.ATTRS_REMAP on a property with TypeError. Properties have three independent accessors (fget, fset, fdel); there is no single callable to forward to. Delegate in each accessor body as shown above.

docs.title: The void(...) Helper
docs.text:
When @deprecated forwards to a target callable, the deprecated function's body never runs — every call is intercepted before the body executes. This creates a practical annoyance: IDEs and linters see the parameters in the signature but nothing using them in the body, and they flag them as unused.

void(...) is a no-op that accepts any arguments and returns None. Its only job is to silence those IDE warnings by giving the parameters a nominal "use" that says: the body is intentionally empty, not accidentally incomplete. It has no runtime effect.

docs.title: When to use void(...)
docs.text:
Use void(...) when all three of these are true:

  • The deprecated function forwards to a target callable (not TargetMode.NOTIFY or TargetMode.ARGS_REMAP).
  • Your IDE or linter flags the function parameters as unused.
  • You want the code to clearly signal that the empty body is deliberate.

If you prefer, a bare pass or a standalone docstring are equally valid. pyDeprecate does not require void(...). Use whichever form is clearest for your team.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
void(...) appears as the return expression of a deprecated wrapper. The call to add is forwarded to add_values immediately, so the return void(a, b) line is never reached. It tells the IDE that a and b are intentionally accepted and ignored.

# NEW API — adds two integers and returns the sum
def add_values(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b


# ---------------------------

from deprecate import deprecated, void


# DEPRECATED API — `add` replaced by `add_values`
@deprecated(target=add_values, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return void(a, b)  # Tells IDE: "Yes, I know these parameters aren't used"
    # This line is never reached - call is forwarded to add_values


# Alternative: You can also use pass or just a docstring
@deprecated(target=add_values, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def add_v1(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Just a docstring works too."""
    pass  # This also works


print(add_v1(2, 3))
Output: add_v1(2, 3) 
5

docs.title: Alternatives to void(...)
docs.text: There are three common patterns for the body of a deprecated function that forwards to a target. All are equivalent at runtime because the body is never reached. The choice is about communicating intent to readers and static analysis.

docs.title: Option 1: pass statement
docs.text:
pass is the simplest approach and clear, idiomatic Python for "do nothing". IDEs may still flag the parameters as unused since nothing references them.

from deprecate import deprecated


# NEW API — evaluates the sum of two integers
def evaluate(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x + y


# DEPRECATED API — `compute` replaced by `evaluate`
@deprecated(target=evaluate, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def compute(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    pass


print(compute(2, 3))
Output: compute(2, 3) 
5

docs.title: Option 2: Docstring-only body
docs.text:
A docstring alone is a valid function body. It is useful when you want to document what the deprecated function did historically or provide migration notes inline.

from deprecate import deprecated


# NEW API — evaluates the sum of two integers
def evaluate(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x + y


# DEPRECATED API — `compute` replaced by `evaluate`
@deprecated(target=evaluate, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def compute(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    """Previously computed x + y. Use evaluate() directly."""


print(compute(2, 3))
Output: compute(2, 3) 
5

docs.title: Option 3: void(...) call
docs.text:
void(...) references all parameters explicitly, silencing "unused parameter" warnings in PyCharm, VS Code (Pylance), and ruff. It also serves as a visual marker that the empty body is intentional.

from deprecate import deprecated, void


# NEW API — evaluates the sum of two integers
def evaluate(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x + y


# DEPRECATED API — `compute` replaced by `evaluate`
@deprecated(target=evaluate, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def compute(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return void(x, y)


print(compute(2, 3))
Output: compute(2, 3) 
5

docs.title: Comparison summary
docs.text:
Approach Silences unused-param warnings Self-documenting intent Extra import pass No Moderate No Docstring only No High (can explain why) No void(...) Yes High (explicit no-op) Yes (from deprecate import void)

If you use a strict linter that flags unused parameters (e.g. ruff's ARG001), void(...) is the cleanest solution that does not require # noqa comments.

docs.title: void(...) in generator stubs
docs.text:
A deprecated generator stub must still contain yield. The wrapper kind follows the stub.

A plain stub gets a plain wrapper

A stub whose body is only return void(...) is a plain function. Its wrapper is therefore a plain function that warns at call time. inspect.isgeneratorfunction reports False, even when the target is a generator.

Call void(...) as a statement and add yield from () so the stub stays a generator function. See Advanced for a full example.

docs.title: void(...) with methods
docs.text:
void(...) works identically in class methods. Reference self and all parameters when forwarding a deprecated method:

from deprecate import deprecated, void


class ImageProcessor:
    def resize(self, width: int, height: int, interpolation: str = "bilinear") -> str:
        return f"Resized to {width}x{height} ({interpolation})"

    @deprecated(target=resize, deprecated_in="2.0", remove_in="3.0")
    def scale(self, width: int, height: int, interpolation: str = "bilinear") -> str:
        """Deprecated — renamed to resize()."""
        return void(width, height, interpolation)


proc = ImageProcessor()
print(proc.scale(800, 600))
Output: proc.scale(800, 600) 
Resized to 800x600 (bilinear)

You do not need to pass self to void(...) — only the parameters your linter flags. self is implicitly used by method dispatch and is never flagged.

docs.title: Type annotation note
docs.text:
No action needed in most cases

Modern versions of mypy and pyright handle decorated functions correctly and do not flag the return type mismatch in dead code paths. The workarounds below are only needed if your type checker explicitly complains.

void(...) returns None, which looks incompatible with a function annotated as -> int. In practice this is fine because:

  1. The body never runs. @deprecated intercepts the call and forwards to the target before the body executes. The return void(...) line is dead code.
  2. Type checkers handle dead code leniently. Since mypy and pyright can see the decorator, they generally do not flag return type mismatches in unreachable paths.
  3. If your type checker does complain, two workarounds:
from deprecate import deprecated, void
from typing import Any, cast


# NEW API — doubles the input value; replaces the deprecated score wrappers
def score_predictions(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2


# Option A: Use `pass` instead (no return statement at all)
# DEPRECATED API — `transform_a` replaced by `score_predictions`
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def transform_a(x: int) -> int:
    pass  # type: ignore[return-value]


# Option B: Cast the void return (technically dead code)
# DEPRECATED API — `transform_b` replaced by `score_predictions`
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def transform_b(x: int) -> int:
    return cast(int, void(x))


print(transform_b(2))
Output: transform_b(2) 
4

In practice, neither workaround is usually needed — modern versions of mypy handle decorated functions correctly and do not flag unreachable return statements.

docs.title: void(...) vs assert_no_warnings
docs.text:
These two utilities solve completely different problems. Their names might suggest a connection, but they operate in different contexts. assert_no_warnings is a test-time tool covered in Testing Deprecated Code.

void(...) assert_no_warnings() Purpose Silence IDE "unused parameter" warnings in function bodies Assert that no warnings of a given type are emitted during a code block Where used Inside the body of a deprecated function stub In test code, as a context manager Runtime effect None (accepts args, returns None) Captures warnings and raises AssertionError if any match Import from deprecate import void from deprecate import assert_no_warnings 
from deprecate import deprecated, void, assert_no_warnings


# NEW API — doubles the input value
def score_predictions(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2


# void() — used in the deprecated function body (decoration-time concern)
# DEPRECATED API — `score` replaced by `score_predictions`
@deprecated(target=score_predictions, deprecated_in="1.0", remove_in="2.0")
def score(x: int) -> int:
    return void(x)


# assert_no_warnings — used in tests (runtime assertion concern)
with assert_no_warnings(FutureWarning):
    # Verify that calling the NEW function does not trigger any deprecation warning
    result = score_predictions(42)
print(result)
Output: score_predictions(42) 
84
